docs.title: PHP Security Basics — SQL Injection, XSS, CSRF & Password Hashing
docs.meta_title: PHP Security Basics | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: The four security issues every PHP developer runs into eventually — SQL injection, cross-site scripting, CSRF, and how to store passwords safely — and how to actually prevent each one.

blocks.html: PHP scripts commonly handle user input, a database, and a login system — which means they're also commonly the target of a handful of well-understood attacks. Each one has a specific, practical defense.

Building a query by directly inserting user input into the SQL string lets an attacker inject their own SQL — the earlier MySQL lessons' use of PDO prepared statements is exactly what prevents this, and it's worth understanding why.

String-concatenating any user input directly into a SQL query is the single most common serious PHP security bug. A prepared statement isn't an optional improvement — treat it as mandatory for every query that includes user input.
blocks.title: The one rule that matters most here

blocks.html: If user input is echoed back into a page without escaping it, an attacker can submit HTML or JavaScript that runs in another visitor's browser — stealing their session, or acting on their behalf.
The rule of thumb: escape on output, every time, with htmlspecialchars() — not just for input that "looks risky." It costs nothing when the input was harmless anyway.
blocks.title: Escape everything, not just the suspicious parts

blocks.html: Without protection, a malicious site can trick a logged-in user's browser into submitting a form to your site — the browser automatically includes the user's session cookie, making the request look legitimate. A CSRF token defeats this: a random value stored in the session and required on every form submission.
A password must never be stored as plain text or with a simple hash like MD5 — PHP's built-in password_hash() uses a strong, salted, deliberately slow algorithm designed specifically for this.

rows: Prepared statements — never concatenate input into SQL
htmlspecialchars() on every piece of output that includes user input
A random token in the session, checked on every state-changing form submission
password_hash() to store, password_verify() to check

blocks.html: This lesson covers the specific PHP-level defenses. The Cybersecurity course elsewhere on this site covers phishing, password managers, and account security from the user's side — worth pairing with this one.
blocks.title: Related, from the other side

docs.title: OOP — Namespaces
docs.meta_title: PHP Namespaces | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Organizing classes into named groups to avoid naming collisions, especially once a project uses external packages.

blocks.html: As soon as a project has more than a handful of classes — or uses any external package (covered in the Composer lesson ahead) — two classes with the same name is a real risk. A namespace prevents that collision.
A namespace declaration must be the very first statement in a PHP file.

blocks.code:
<?php
namespace App\Models;

class User {
    // this class's full name is App\Models\User
}

<?php
namespace App\Models;
class User { /* ... */ }

namespace App\Auth;
class User { /* ... */ }   // a completely different class,
                            // fully named App\Auth\User —
                            // no naming conflict at all

blocks.text: Using a Class from Another Namespace — use

blocks.code:
<?php
namespace App\Controllers;

use App\Models\User;

$user = new User();   // resolves to App\Models\User

blocks.html: Useful when two classes from different namespaces would otherwise share the same short name.

The convention followed by nearly every modern PHP project — and the one Composer's autoloading (next lesson) expects — is one namespace matching the folder structure: App\Models\User lives in app/Models/User.php.
blocks.title: Namespaces usually mirror folders

toc.text: Using a Class from Another Namespace — use

docs.title: OOP — Magic Methods
docs.meta_title: PHP Magic Methods | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: PHP's special __-prefixed methods that run automatically for certain operations — reading an undefined property, converting an object to a string, and more.

blocks.html: PHP calls a small set of specially-named methods automatically, in response to specific operations on an object — reading a property that doesn't exist, treating an object as a string, and a few others. __construct() from earlier lessons is the most common one; here are the rest worth knowing.

blocks.text: __toString() — Converting an Object to a String
__get() and __set() — Reading and Writing Undefined Properties

blocks.html: Runs when code tries to read or write a property that isn't explicitly declared — useful for computed or dynamically-stored properties.

blocks.text: __call() — Handling a Call to an Undefined Method

rows: An object is destroyed or the script ends
An object is used in a string context (echo, concatenation)
An undefined property is read or written

blocks.html: Magic methods make code harder to trace — a click-to-definition on $config->siteName won't lead anywhere obvious. Use them for a genuine, specific need (a config object, a lightweight ORM), not as a default way to write a class.
blocks.title: A real trade-off, not a free upgrade

docs.title: OOP — Polymorphism and Type Declarations
docs.meta_title: PHP Polymorphism and Type Declarations | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Calling the same method on different object types and getting each one's own correct behavior — and the type declarations that make code relying on this safe.

blocks.html: Polymorphism means code can call the same method name on different types of objects, and each one runs its own version — the earlier Interfaces lesson already builds this in practice; this lesson names the concept and covers the type declarations that make it safe to rely on.

blocks.text: Why the Type Hint Matters Here

blocks.html: The Shape $shape parameter type is what makes this safe — PHP guarantees anything passed in has an area() method, without printArea needing to check what kind of shape it received.

rows: Union type — more than one allowed

blocks.text: A Brief Note on Dependency Injection

blocks.html: Type-hinting an interface, as printArea(Shape $shape) does, is also the foundation of dependency injection — a class that depends on an interface rather than one specific class can have any matching implementation "injected" into it, which is what makes swapping a real database for a test double possible without changing the class itself. It's a full topic on its own, worth knowing the name and the idea now.
PHP checks types at runtime, not compile time — a wrong type still causes an error, just when that line of code actually runs rather than before the script starts.
blocks.title: PHP's typing is runtime-checked

docs.title: Making HTTP Requests with cURL
docs.meta_title: PHP cURL Requests | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Calling another server's API from PHP with cURL — GET and POST requests, sending JSON, and reading the response.

blocks.html: A PHP script often needs to talk to another service — a payment provider, a weather API, a third-party service's data. cURL is PHP's built-in way to make that outgoing HTTP request.

rows: Returns the response as a string instead of printing it directly
Sends the request as POST instead of GET
The data to send in a POST request
An array of custom headers, like Content-Type or Authorization
Maximum seconds to wait before giving up

blocks.html: A network failure — a timeout, a DNS error — needs to be checked for separately from a bad HTTP status code.

The Guzzle package (installed via Composer, from the earlier lesson) wraps cURL in a much friendlier API and is the standard choice for a real project — raw cURL is still worth understanding since it's what Guzzle itself uses underneath.

docs.title: Composer and Autoloading
docs.meta_title: PHP Composer and Autoloading | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: PHP's package manager — installing a library, managing dependencies, and letting classes load automatically without a manual require for each one.

blocks.html: Composer is PHP's standard package manager — it installs and manages external libraries, and (just as usefully) handles loading a project's own classes automatically, without a manual require for every file.

blocks.code: composer require guzzlehttp/guzzle

blocks.html: This downloads the package into a vendor/ folder and records it (with its version) in a composer.json file, so the exact same dependencies can be reinstalled anywhere.
One line, at the top of the entry file, loads every installed package's classes.

blocks.text: Autoloading a Project's Own Classes — PSR-4

blocks.html: The "App\\": "app/" line in composer.json above tells Composer that any class in the App namespace lives in the app/ folder, following the same path — no manual require needed for a project's own files either.
After adding or moving a class, running composer dump-autoload rebuilds the autoloader's internal class map.

blocks.code: composer dump-autoload

rows: Creates a new composer.json for a project
Installs a package and adds it to composer.json
Installs everything listed in composer.json — used when cloning a project
Updates packages to their latest allowed versions
Rebuilds the autoloader after adding/moving classes

blocks.html: Packagist (packagist.org) is the official package registry Composer searches — worth checking there before writing something from scratch that a well-maintained package already solves.
blocks.title: Where packages come from

toc.text: Autoloading a Project's Own Classes — PSR-4

docs.title: Working with JSON in PHP
docs.meta_title: PHP JSON Processing | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Converting a PHP array or object to JSON and back — the standard format for an API request or response.

blocks.html: JSON is the standard format for exchanging data between a PHP backend and a frontend, or between two servers — nearly every API request and response uses it. PHP has JSON support built in, no package required.

blocks.code: echo json_encode($user, JSON_PRETTY_PRINT);

blocks.html: By default, this returns an stdClass object — pass true as the second argument to get an associative array instead, usually the more convenient choice.
Invalid JSON makes json_decode() return null — worth checking explicitly, since a genuinely empty result also decodes to something falsy.
Not every PHP value converts cleanly — a resource (like an open file handle) can't be represented in JSON at all, and encoding one silently produces 0 rather than an error.
blocks.title: What json_encode() can't do

docs.title: Environment Variables and Configuration
docs.meta_title: PHP Environment Variables | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Keeping secrets and per-environment settings out of the codebase with environment variables and a .env file.

blocks.html: A database password, an API key, or a setting that differs between a local machine and a live server doesn't belong hardcoded in a PHP file — an environment variable keeps it outside the codebase entirely.
A plain text file, kept out of version control, listing key-value pairs — the standard way to set environment variables on a local machine without configuring the whole OS.

blocks.code:
# .env
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_NAME=myapp
DB_USER=root
DB_PASSWORD=secret123
API_KEY=sk_test_abc123

blocks.html: PHP doesn't read .env files natively — the standard package for it, installed via Composer, loads the file's values into getenv()/$_ENV.

blocks.code: composer require vlucas/phpdotenv

# .gitignore
.env

blocks.html: A .env file committed to a public repository is one of the most common real-world causes of a leaked API key or database password — add it to .gitignore from the very first commit, not after the fact.
blocks.title: The most important habit in this lesson

blocks.html: A version of the file with the keys but placeholder values, committed to the repo — shows every teammate what variables are needed, without exposing any real secret.

blocks.code:
# .env.example — safe to commit
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_NAME=
DB_USER=
DB_PASSWORD=
API_KEY=

docs.title: WordPress Hooks — Actions and Filters
docs.meta_title: WordPress Hooks — Actions and Filters | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: The system behind almost every functions.php snippet in this course — how actions and filters work, and how to define a custom hook of your own.

blocks.html: Nearly every earlier lesson's functions.php code used add_action() — enqueuing assets, registering a menu, setting up theme support — without fully explaining the system underneath it. This lesson covers that system directly: WordPress's hooks, the mechanism that lets a theme (or plugin) run code at a specific point without editing WordPress's own core files.

rows: Run some code at a specific point — no return value expected
Modify a piece of data and hand it back — always returns a value

blocks.text: An Action — Run Code at a Specific Moment

blocks.html: after_setup_theme is the hook name — a specific moment WordPress reaches during every page load. add_action() attaches wgh_setup_theme to run at that exact moment.

blocks.text: A Filter — Modify a Value and Return It

blocks.html: Unlike an action, a filter's function always receives a value and must return one — often the same value, changed.

blocks.text: Defining a Custom Hook — do_action() and apply_filters()

blocks.html: Themes and plugins don't just use WordPress's built-in hooks — they can define their own, letting other code (a child theme, a plugin) extend a specific point without editing the original file.
remove_action() and remove_filter() undo a hook — useful when a parent theme's behavior needs to be disabled from a child theme, covered in the next lesson.

blocks.code: remove_action('wp_head', 'wp_generator');   // hides the WordPress version number from the page source

blocks.html: A fast way to spot which hook to use for a given task: search the specific WordPress or plugin function's entry on developer.wordpress.org — its "Hooks" section lists every action and filter that fires inside it.
blocks.title: Finding the right hook name

docs.title: WordPress Shortcodes
docs.meta_title: WordPress Shortcodes | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Registering a custom [bracket] shortcode that outputs reusable HTML, so an editor typing into a post never needs to touch PHP.

blocks.html: A shortcode is a small bracketed tag — [shortcode] — typed directly into a post or page's content, which WordPress replaces with dynamically generated HTML when the page renders. It's a way to hand a piece of reusable PHP output to an editor who never touches code.
A shortcode can accept attributes, just like an HTML tag — shortcode_atts() merges them with sensible defaults.
A shortcode written with an opening and closing tag receives whatever's between them as its second argument.
A shortcode function must return its HTML, never echo it directly — echoing prints the output in the wrong place in the page's render order, usually above the content instead of inside it.
blocks.title: return, not echo

blocks.text: Using a Shortcode Inside a Template

blocks.html: Outside a post's content, a shortcode needs to be run through do_shortcode() explicitly.

blocks.code: <?php echo do_shortcode('[button text="Contact Us" url="/contact"]'); ?>

toc.text: Using a Shortcode Inside a Template

docs.title: Child Themes
docs.meta_title: WordPress Child Themes | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Customizing or extending an existing theme safely — changes that survive the parent theme's next update.

blocks.html: Editing a theme's files directly works, until the theme gets updated — every direct edit is silently overwritten. A child theme inherits everything from a parent theme while keeping customizations in a separate folder the update process never touches.
Just two files are required — a stylesheet declaring the relationship, and a functions file.
The Template: line — matching the parent theme's folder name exactly — is what makes it a child theme rather than a standalone one.
A child theme's own style.css replaces the parent's entirely by default — its CSS needs to be loaded explicitly, then the child's own rules enqueued after it to override anything needed.

rows: The active theme's folder — the child theme, if one is active

blocks.html: Placing a file with the exact same name and path in the child theme overrides just that one file — every other template still comes from the parent, unchanged.

blocks.code:
my-child-theme/
├── style.css
├── functions.php
└── single.php    ← only this template is overridden; page.php, index.php, etc. still load from the parent

blocks.html: A child theme is the standard, safe way to make any change to a theme not built for the site — including a purchased or downloaded theme whose updates need to keep working normally.
blocks.title: When to reach for one

docs.title: Widgets and Widget-Ready Sidebars
docs.meta_title: WordPress Widgets and Sidebars | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Registering a widget-ready area in a theme, and outputting it in a template — the classic-theme way to give an editor a drag-and-drop content area.

blocks.html: A widget area (also called a "sidebar" in the WordPress API, regardless of where it's actually placed on the page) is a region a theme defines, that an editor can then fill with content blocks from the WordPress admin — without touching any code.
Wrapped in a check for whether the area actually has any widgets placed in it — an empty sidebar shouldn't render an empty wrapper element.

blocks.code:
<?php if (is_active_sidebar('blog-sidebar')) : ?>
    <aside class="sidebar">
        <?php dynamic_sidebar('blog-sidebar'); ?>
    </aside>
<?php endif; ?>

blocks.text: before_widget and before_title — What They're For

blocks.html: Every widget an editor drags into this area gets automatically wrapped in the HTML defined by these four settings — a consistent container and heading structure without the theme needing to know in advance which widgets will be used.
Since WordPress 5.8, a widget area can also hold blocks (the same block editor used for post content), not just the older classic widgets — register_sidebar() itself is unchanged either way.
blocks.title: Widgets and the block editor

toc.text: before_widget and before_title — What They're For

docs.title: Nonces and Form Security
docs.meta_title: WordPress Nonces and Form Security | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Verifying a form submission or action actually came from your site's own page, not a forged request from somewhere else.

blocks.html: The earlier Escaping & Sanitizing lesson covered making output safe. A nonce ("number used once") covers the other direction — verifying an incoming form submission or action request genuinely came from a page your site rendered, not a forged request from elsewhere.

Without one, a malicious site could trick a logged-in user's browser into submitting a request to your site — the browser sends the session cookie automatically, making the forged request look legitimate. This is the same CSRF attack covered in the PHP Security lesson; a nonce is WordPress's specific built-in defense against it.

blocks.text: Adding a Nonce to a Form

blocks.code:
<form method="post" action="">
    <?php wp_nonce_field('wgh_save_settings', 'wgh_nonce'); ?>
    <input type="text" name="site_tagline">
    <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>

blocks.html: wp_nonce_field() outputs a hidden input containing a token tied to the current user's session and the action name given as its first argument.

blocks.text: Nonces in a URL — for a Link-Triggered Action

blocks.html: The same idea applies to a plain link that triggers an action (deleting an item, for example), not just a form.

blocks.code: Delete

blocks.html: A nonce expires (24 hours by default) and is tied to the specific user session that generated it — it isn't a password or a secret to keep hidden, just a check that the request came from where it claims to.
blocks.title: What a nonce is not

docs.title: The JavaScript Event Loop
docs.meta_title: The JavaScript Event Loop | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Why JavaScript can run asynchronous code with only one thread — the call stack, the task queue, and how the event loop connects them.

blocks.html: JavaScript runs on a single thread — it can only do one thing at a time. Yet a page can wait on a network request, a timer, and a click handler all at once, without freezing. The event loop is the mechanism that makes this possible.
Every function call gets pushed onto the call stack, and popped off when it returns. JavaScript only ever runs what's on top of the stack.
A function like setTimeout hands its callback off to the browser, not the call stack — the call stack stays free to keep running the rest of the script immediately.

Once a timer, network request, or event fires, its callback doesn't interrupt the call stack directly — it waits in a queue. The event loop's job is simple: check if the call stack is empty, and if so, move the next callback in queue onto it.

Not all queued callbacks are treated equally. Promise callbacks go into a microtask queue, which the event loop always fully empties before touching the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval, DOM events).

blocks.code:
console.log('1')
setTimeout(() => console.log('2 — macrotask'), 0)
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3 — microtask'))
console.log('4')

// Output: 1, 4, 3, 2 — microtasks always run before the next macrotask

rows: Fully drained before the next macrotask
One runs per event loop cycle

blocks.html: This site's Event Loop tool (under Tools) animates the call stack, task queue, and microtask queue step by step for a piece of code — a much faster way to build intuition than reading the ordering rules alone.
blocks.title: Practice it interactively

docs.title: Recursion in JavaScript
docs.meta_title: Recursion in JavaScript | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: A function calling itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem — the base case, the call stack it builds, and when to reach for it.

blocks.html: Recursion is a function solving a problem by calling itself with a smaller version of that same problem, until it reaches a version simple enough to answer directly.

blocks.text: The Base Case Is Not Optional

blocks.html: Without a condition that stops it, a recursive function calls itself forever — or more precisely, until the call stack runs out of room.

Every recursive function needs a base case that's actually reachable — a base case that never triggers (a wrong comparison, an argument that never converges toward it) fails exactly the same way as no base case at all.
blocks.title: The most common recursion bug

blocks.text: What the Call Stack Looks Like

blocks.html: Each recursive call adds a new frame to the call stack (from the earlier Event Loop lesson) — the function doesn't actually finish until every deeper call it made has returned.

rows: Often reads more naturally for a problem that's naturally recursive (traversing a tree, nested data)
Usually faster and uses less memory for a simple repeated task
Each call adds a call stack frame — deep recursion can hit a stack size limit
No stack depth concern regardless of how many iterations

blocks.html: This site's Recursion tool (under Tools) visualizes the call tree unwinding step by step for a piece of code — a clearer way to see what "each call waits for the next" actually looks like than tracing it by hand.
blocks.title: Practice it interactively

docs.title: Prototypes and Prototypal Inheritance
docs.meta_title: Prototypes and Prototypal Inheritance | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: What the class keyword is actually built on top of — the prototype chain that lets one object inherit properties and methods from another.

blocks.html: The earlier Classes and OOP lesson used the class keyword — but underneath it, JavaScript objects don't use classes the way other languages do. They use prototypes, and class is really a friendlier syntax built on top of that older system.
An object's prototype is another object it automatically looks up properties and methods on, when it doesn't have one of its own.

blocks.code:
const animal = {
  eats: true,
}

const rabbit = Object.create(animal)   // rabbit's prototype is animal
rabbit.jumps = true

console.log(rabbit.jumps)   // true — rabbit's own property
console.log(rabbit.eats)    // true — found on animal, its prototype

blocks.html: If a property isn't found on the prototype either, JavaScript keeps looking up the prototype's own prototype, and so on, until it reaches null — this chain is why it's called prototypal inheritance.

blocks.text: Where a Constructor Function's Methods Actually Live
class Is Prototypes, With Cleaner Syntax

blocks.html: A class method is stored on the prototype exactly the same way — class doesn't replace the prototype system, it's a more readable way to write to it.

Every object created from a class or constructor function shares one copy of each method on the prototype — this is why methods (unlike properties set in the constructor) don't take extra memory per object.
blocks.title: Why methods live on the prototype, not each object

toc.text: Where a Constructor Function's Methods Actually Live
class Is Prototypes, With Cleaner Syntax

docs.title: Generators and Iterators
docs.meta_title: Generators and Iterators | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: What makes for...of work on arrays and strings, and generator functions that can pause mid-execution and resume later.

blocks.html: An iterator is what lets for...of and the spread operator work on something — a protocol any object can implement. A generator is a special kind of function that builds an iterator automatically, and can pause its own execution.
Arrays, strings, Maps, and Sets are all iterable — they implement Symbol.iterator, a method that returns an object with a next() method producing one value at a time.
for...of is really just repeatedly calling next() under the hood, stopping when done becomes true.
A generator, marked with function*, pauses at every yield and resumes exactly where it left off the next time it's called.
Since a generator automatically implements the iterator protocol, it works directly with for...of and the spread operator.

blocks.text: A Practical Use — Lazy, On-Demand Values

blocks.html: Because a generator only computes the next value when asked, it can represent a sequence too large — or infinite — to build all at once.
A generator's pause-and-resume behavior is also the mechanism async/await is built on top of, conceptually — both let a function stop mid-execution and continue later without blocking anything else.
blocks.title: The connection to async/await

toc.text: A Practical Use — Lazy, On-Demand Values

docs.title: Map, Set, WeakMap, and WeakSet
docs.meta_title: JavaScript Map and Set | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Four built-in data structures beyond plain objects and arrays — a Map for any-type keys, a Set for unique values, and their memory-friendly Weak variants.

blocks.html: A plain object and array cover most needs, but four more built-in structures solve specific problems neither one does well.
A plain object's keys are always converted to strings. A Map allows a key of any type — an object, a function, even another Map.
A Set stores a list of values with duplicates automatically removed.

blocks.text: A Practical Use for Set — Deduplicating an Array

blocks.html: WeakMap and WeakSet work like their non-weak counterparts, but only accept objects as keys/values, and don't prevent those objects from being garbage collected (covered in the earlier Memory Management lesson) once nothing else references them. This makes them useful for attaching extra data to an object without causing a memory leak.

toc.text: A Practical Use for Set — Deduplicating an Array

docs.title: Rest and Spread Operators
docs.meta_title: JavaScript Rest and Spread Operators | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: The same ... syntax doing two opposite jobs — collecting multiple values into an array, or expanding an array into individual values.

blocks.html: The ... syntax does one of two opposite things depending on where it's used: rest collects several values into one array, spread expands one array (or object) into several values.
Gathers any number of remaining arguments into a real array — a modern replacement for the older, array-like arguments object.

blocks.code:
const a = [1, 2, 3]
const b = [4, 5, 6]
const combined = [...a, ...b]
// [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

Math.max(...a)   // 3 — spreads the array into separate arguments

rows: Rest — collects arguments into an array
...arr inside an array or function call
Spread — expands an array into individual values
Spread — copies an object's own properties

blocks.html: Object spread ({ ...original, updatedField: value }) is the standard way to update state immutably in React and similar frameworks — worth being comfortable with this syntax before that course.
blocks.title: Where this shows up next

docs.title: Memory Management and Garbage Collection
docs.meta_title: JavaScript Memory Management | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: How JavaScript allocates and frees memory automatically, and the common patterns that accidentally prevent memory from ever being freed.

blocks.html: Unlike some languages, JavaScript never requires manually freeing memory — a garbage collector does it automatically. Understanding roughly how it decides what to free explains most real-world memory leaks.

rows: Memory is reserved when a value is created — a variable, an object, a function
The program reads and writes to that memory
The garbage collector frees the memory once nothing can reach it anymore

blocks.text: Reachability — How the Garbage Collector Decides

blocks.html: An object is kept in memory as long as it's reachable — reachable directly or indirectly from a "root" (global variables, the current call stack). The instant nothing references an object anymore, it becomes eligible for collection.
A running setInterval keeps everything its callback references reachable, indefinitely, until explicitly cleared — even if the code that created it is long gone.

blocks.text: A Common Leak — Detached DOM References

blocks.html: A removed DOM element still can't be garbage collected if a variable somewhere still references it.

blocks.text: A Common Leak — Forgotten Event Listeners

blocks.html: The Memory tab in browser DevTools can take a heap snapshot and compare it over time — a growing number of detached DOM nodes between snapshots is the clearest practical sign of a real leak.
blocks.title: Checking for a leak in practice

docs.title: The Linux Command Line — A Practical Deep Dive
docs.meta_title: The Linux Command Line — A Practical Deep Dive | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: A long, practical tour of the Linux command line — files, permissions, text processing, processes, users, packages, services, networking, and basic shell scripting.

blocks.html: Linux runs most of the servers on the internet, and its command line appears constantly in security guides, hosting tutorials, and troubleshooting articles — including elsewhere on this site (the Hosting & Deployment course connects to a server over SSH and uses exactly these commands). This lesson is a long, practical tour, deliberately going further than a typical "basics" chapter — the more of this that feels familiar, the less intimidating a real server becomes.

blocks.code:
# Show the current folder
pwd

# List files and folders here
ls -la

# Move into a folder
cd Downloads

# Go back up one level
cd ..

# Go straight to the home folder
cd ~

blocks.html: ls -la specifically — the -a flag shows hidden files (names starting with a dot, like .ssh or .bashrc), which regular ls quietly skips. A surprising amount of security-relevant configuration lives in hidden files.

blocks.text: The Directory Hierarchy — Where Things Live

blocks.html: Unlike Windows' separate drive letters, Linux has one single folder tree starting at / (the root) — everything, including other disks, gets mounted somewhere inside it.

rows: Data that changes often — logs, caches, mail
Installed programs and their supporting files
Temporary files, usually cleared on reboot

blocks.text: Working with Files — Creating, Moving, Deleting

blocks.code:
# Create an empty file
touch notes.txt

# Create a folder
mkdir project

# Copy a file
cp notes.txt backup-notes.txt

# Copy an entire folder
cp -r project project-backup

# Move or rename (same command does both)
mv notes.txt archive/notes.txt
mv old-name.txt new-name.txt

# Delete a file
rm notes.txt

# Delete a folder and everything in it
rm -rf project-backup

blocks.html: rm -rf deletes permanently — no Recycle Bin, no undo. Double-check the path before running it, especially with a wildcard (rm -rf *) or as root.
blocks.title: The most dangerous common command

blocks.code:
# Print a whole file to the screen
cat notes.txt

# Scroll through a long file (q to quit)
less server.log

# First 10 lines
head server.log

# Last 10 lines — great for watching a log grow
tail server.log

# Keep watching a file as new lines are added
tail -f server.log

blocks.html: For actually editing a file from the terminal, nano is the friendliest starting point — arrow keys work as expected, and the shortcuts are listed on screen.

blocks.code:
nano config.txt
# Ctrl+O to save, Ctrl+X to exit

blocks.html: vim is the other common option, far more powerful once learned but genuinely unintuitive at first — it opens in "normal mode," where typing doesn't insert text until i is pressed. Worth knowing at least the exit sequence, since it's a famous first stumbling block.

blocks.code:
vim config.txt
# Press i to start typing (insert mode)
# Press Esc to leave insert mode
# Type :wq and press Enter to save and quit
# Type :q! and press Enter to quit WITHOUT saving

blocks.text: Redirects, Pipes, and the Three I/O Streams

blocks.html: Every command has three data streams: stdin (input), stdout (normal output), and stderr (error output) — understanding these unlocks most of what makes the command line powerful.

rows: Send stdout to a file, overwriting it
Send stdout to a file, appending to it
Feed a file in as stdin
Pipe — send one command's stdout as the next command's stdin

blocks.code:
# Save output to a file
ls -la > filelist.txt

# Append instead of overwrite
echo "new entry" >> notes.txt

# Send errors to a separate file, keep normal output on screen
some-command 2> errors.log

# Chain commands — this pipeline is genuinely common in practice
ps aux | grep nginx | wc -l
# ps aux: list every process
# grep nginx: keep only lines mentioning nginx
# wc -l: count the remaining lines

blocks.text: Text Processing — cut, sort, uniq, grep, awk

blocks.html: Linux's small, single-purpose text tools are designed to be piped together — this is the toolkit behind reading logs, filtering data, and quick one-off reports without writing a script.

rows: Search recursively through every file in a folder
Extract one column from delimited text (here, the 2nd, comma-separated)
Remove adjacent duplicate lines (usually paired with sort first)
Count lines (also -w for words, -c for characters)
Translate characters — here, lowercase to uppercase

blocks.code:
# Find every failed login attempt in an auth log
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log

# Get a sorted, de-duplicated list of IPs that tried
grep "Failed password" /var/log/auth.log | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
# awk pulls out one field per line, sort+uniq -c counts how often
# each IP appears, the final sort -rn ranks the worst offenders first

blocks.html: awk and sed are both full text-processing languages on their own — the single most useful pattern to remember from each: awk '{print $N}' to grab column N of space-separated text, and sed 's/old/new/g' to find-and-replace text in a stream.

blocks.code:
# Replace every occurrence of "staging" with "production" and print the result
sed 's/staging/production/g' config.txt

blocks.html: Every file on Linux has permissions controlling who can read, write, or execute it — this is not a formality, it's an actual access-control mechanism. A world-writable config file or an overly permissive SSH key is a genuine, common vulnerability.

blocks.code:
# Check permissions on a file
ls -l script.sh
# -rwxr-xr-- 1 sam staff 220 Sep 3 10:00 script.sh

blocks.html: That first block of ten characters breaks into: the file type, then three permission triplets (owner, group, everyone else) — each triplet is read (r), write (w), execute (x), or a dash for "not permitted."

blocks.code:
# Give the owner read+write+execute, group read+execute, others nothing
chmod 750 script.sh

# The same change, written symbolically
chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o= script.sh

# Make a file only the owner can read and write (common for SSH keys)
chmod 600 id_rsa

# Change who owns a file
chown sam script.sh

# Change owner and group together
chown sam:staff script.sh

# Bundle a folder into one .tar file
tar -cvf backup.tar project/

# Same, but gzip-compressed (.tar.gz)
tar -czvf backup.tar.gz project/

# Unpack a .tar.gz
tar -xzvf backup.tar.gz

# Zip / unzip, if that format is needed instead
zip -r backup.zip project/
unzip backup.zip

blocks.html: c = create, x = extract, z = gzip, v = verbose (show progress), f = the filename follows.

blocks.code:
# Search by name, from the current folder down
find . -name "*.log"

# Search the whole system for a file modified in the last day
find / -name "config.php" -mtime -1

# Fast search using a pre-built index (usually faster, may be slightly stale)
locate nginx.conf

# List every running process
ps aux

# Live, auto-refreshing view of processes and resource use
top

# End a process by its process ID (find the ID from ps aux first)
kill 4821

# Force-kill a process that ignores a normal kill
kill -9 4821

blocks.html: Ending an unfamiliar process ID can break something else that depends on it. Confirm what a process is (via ps aux or a search on its name) before ending it.
blocks.title: Know before you kill

blocks.code:
# Start a long-running command in the background
long-task &

# List the current background jobs
jobs

# Bring a background job back to the foreground
fg %1

# A command that keeps running even after the terminal closes
nohup long-task &

blocks.html: Every file, process, and permission ultimately belongs to a user — and every user belongs to one or more groups, which is how group-level permissions from the earlier section actually get applied.

blocks.code:
# Add a new user
sudo useradd -m newuser   # -m also creates their home folder

# Set (or change) that user's password
sudo passwd newuser

# Add an existing user to a group
sudo usermod -aG developers newuser

# See which groups the current user belongs to
groups

# Delete a user (and optionally their home folder with -r)
sudo userdel -r newuser

blocks.text: sudo — Running One Command as Another User

blocks.html: sudo runs a single command with administrator (root) privileges, rather than logging in as root directly — the safer, standard approach, since it's scoped to one command and logged.

blocks.code:
sudo apt update

# Run a shell as root (use sparingly)
sudo -i

blocks.html: Installing software on Linux almost never means downloading an installer — a package manager handles finding, installing, updating, and removing software from a trusted repository.

rows: sudo apt install <package> / sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade
sudo dnf install <package> / sudo dnf update

blocks.code:
# Update the local list of available packages
sudo apt update

# Install a package
sudo apt install htop

# Remove a package
sudo apt remove htop

# List installed packages
apt list --installed

# Upgrade every installed package
sudo apt upgrade

blocks.html: Most modern Linux distributions manage background services (a web server, a database, an SSH server) with systemd, via the systemctl command.

blocks.code:
# Check whether a service is running
sudo systemctl status nginx

# Start / stop / restart a service
sudo systemctl start nginx
sudo systemctl stop nginx
sudo systemctl restart nginx

# Make a service start automatically on boot
sudo systemctl enable nginx

# Read a service's recent logs
journalctl -u nginx --since today

blocks.text: Environment Variables and the Command Path

blocks.html: An environment variable is a named value available to every program run in that session — PATH is the most important one, since it's the list of folders the shell searches when a command is typed without a full path.

blocks.code:
# Show every environment variable
env

# Show one specific variable
echo $HOME
echo $PATH

# Set one for the current session only
export API_KEY=abc123

# Set one permanently — added to ~/.bashrc (or ~/.zshrc), then re-loaded
echo 'export API_KEY=abc123' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc

# Show this machine's IP address
ip a

# Test whether a host is reachable
ping -c 4 google.com

# Trace the network hops to a host
traceroute google.com

# List active network connections and the process using each
ss -tulnp

# The older equivalent, still common in guides
netstat -tulnp

# Download a file or check an API from the command line
curl -I https://example.com    # -I: headers only
wget https://example.com/file.zip

# Look up a domain's DNS records
dig example.com
nslookup example.com

blocks.html: ss -tulnp is worth remembering on its own — it lists every port a program is listening on, which is exactly what to check when trying to work out whether something unexpected is running a server on a machine.

blocks.code:
# Show disk space used per mounted filesystem
df -h

# Show how much space a specific folder is using
du -sh /var/log

# List the block devices (drives and partitions) attached
lsblk

# Show what's currently mounted where
mount

blocks.html: Any sequence of commands can be saved into a file and run as a script — the same commands covered throughout this lesson, just automated.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/bash
# The line above is the "shebang" — tells the system which
# interpreter to run this file with

name="World"
echo "Hello, $name!"

chmod +x greet.sh   # make it executable
./greet.sh          # run it

# A variable
count=5

# A conditional
if [ "$count" -gt 3 ]; then
  echo "More than 3"
else
  echo "3 or fewer"
fi

# A loop
for file in *.txt; do
  echo "Found: $file"
done

blocks.html: A quick, standard set of checks for "what's going on with this machine" — worth knowing as a sequence, not just individually.

blocks.code:
# How long has this system been up, and how loaded is it?
uptime

# Who is (or has recently been) logged in?
who
last

# What does the system log say happened recently?
tail -50 /var/log/syslog       # Debian/Ubuntu
journalctl -n 50                # systemd-based systems

# The most recent kernel/hardware messages
dmesg | tail -50

# How much memory is free?
free -h

rows: Is a specific service actually running?
List files and folders, including hidden ones
View a file — all at once, scrollable, first lines, last lines
grep / awk / sed / cut / sort / uniq
Network configuration, connectivity, requests, open ports
Disk space, folder size, attached drives

blocks.html: Deliberately left out of this lesson: containers (Docker), advanced storage (LVM), deep networking internals (the full TCP/IP stack, Netfilter/iptables rule-writing), and boot process internals — genuinely useful, but DevOps/sysadmin-specialist territory rather than the security-relevant CLI literacy this course is scoped for.
blocks.title: What this deliberately leaves out

docs.title: Data Constraints — FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK
docs.meta_title: SQL Data Constraints | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: The rules a table enforces on its own data beyond PRIMARY KEY — a foreign key linking tables, uniqueness, required values, and custom conditions.

blocks.html: The earlier DDL lesson's CREATE TABLE examples used PRIMARY KEY to uniquely identify each row. Four more constraints enforce rules on the data itself — the database refuses any change that would break them, rather than trusting the application to check.
Ensures a column's value must already exist as a primary key in another table — the mechanism that actually connects related tables together.

• Prevents an order from ever referencing a customer that doesn't exist.
  • Also blocks deleting a customer who still has orders, unless the table explicitly allows it (e.g. ON DELETE CASCADE).
Forgetting a foreign key doesn't cause an immediate error — it just silently allows "orphaned" rows that reference nothing, discovered much later as confusing bugs.
blocks.title: Common Mistake

blocks.html:
• Unlike PRIMARY KEY, a table can have several UNIQUE columns.
  • Unlike PRIMARY KEY, a UNIQUE column can allow one NULL value (behavior varies slightly by database).

blocks.text: NOT NULL — A Value Is Required

blocks.html: A column with no NOT NULL constraint silently accepts NULL — a very common source of "why is this field empty" bugs traced back to a missing constraint, not application logic.
blocks.title: Common Mistake

blocks.html: Enforces any boolean condition on a column's value — the most flexible constraint.

rows: Uniquely identifies each row, never NULL (covered in the earlier DDL lesson)
A value must exist as a primary key in another table
No two rows share the same value in this column
A value is required — cannot be left empty
A custom condition the value must satisfy

toc.text: NOT NULL — A Value Is Required

docs.title: Self Join and Cross Join
docs.meta_title: SQL Self Join and Cross Join | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Two more join types beyond INNER/LEFT/RIGHT/FULL — a table joined to itself, and every possible combination of two tables' rows.

blocks.html: The earlier Joins lesson covered INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL — every one of them combining rows from two different tables. These last two joins are a bit different.

blocks.text: SELF JOIN — A Table Joined to Itself

blocks.html: Not a distinct join type in SQL syntax — any of the earlier joins (usually INNER or LEFT) used on a table paired with itself, under two different aliases. The classic use case: a table where one row references another row in the same table, like an employee referencing their manager.

• The same table appears twice in the FROM/JOIN clauses, each with its own alias (e and m here).
  • LEFT JOIN, rather than INNER, keeps employees with no manager (like the CEO) in the results, with a NULL manager.
Forgetting to alias the two copies of the table makes it impossible for the query to know which "id" or "name" is being referred to — this is the one join type where an alias isn't optional.
blocks.title: Common Mistake

blocks.html: Combines every row in one table with every row in another — no matching condition at all. A table of 3 rows CROSS JOINed with a table of 4 rows produces 12 rows.

blocks.code:
SELECT sizes.size, colors.color
FROM sizes
CROSS JOIN colors;
-- If sizes has S/M/L and colors has Red/Blue,
-- this produces all 6 combinations: S-Red, S-Blue, M-Red, M-Blue, L-Red, L-Blue

blocks.html:
• Genuinely useful for generating every combination — a product's size/color variants, a calendar of every date times every store location.
  • On two large tables, the row count multiplies fast — a CROSS JOIN on two 10,000-row tables produces 100 million rows.

rows: A regular join (INNER/LEFT/etc.), just on the same table twice
Every row × every row — no matching condition

toc.text: SELF JOIN — A Table Joined to Itself

docs.title: Conditional Expressions — CASE, COALESCE, NULLIF
docs.meta_title: SQL Conditional Expressions | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Branching logic inside a query — CASE for if/else-style output, COALESCE for a NULL fallback, and NULLIF to turn a specific value into NULL.

blocks.html: Some values need to change shape based on a condition, right inside the query, without a separate step in application code afterward. These three expressions cover nearly every case that comes up.

blocks.text: CASE — If/Else Logic in a Query

blocks.html: Evaluates conditions in order and returns the value tied to the first one that matches, falling back to ELSE if none do.

blocks.code:
SELECT
  name,
  price,
  CASE
    WHEN price < 10 THEN 'Budget'
    WHEN price < 50 THEN 'Mid-range'
    ELSE 'Premium'
  END AS price_tier
FROM products;

blocks.html:
• Conditions are checked top to bottom — the first matching WHEN wins, later ones are never checked.
  • ELSE is optional — without it, a row matching no condition gets NULL.

Conditions that overlap can silently return the wrong branch — a common mistake is ordering price ranges so a later, more specific condition never gets reached because an earlier, broader one already matched.
blocks.title: Common Mistake

blocks.html: Takes any number of arguments and returns the first one that isn't NULL — most often used to substitute a default when a value is missing.

blocks.code:
SELECT
  name,
  COALESCE(nickname, name) AS display_name
FROM users;
-- Shows the nickname if one exists, otherwise falls back to the real name

blocks.text: NULLIF — Turn a Specific Value Into NULL

blocks.html: The reverse idea — compares two values, and returns NULL if they're equal, or the first value otherwise. Most commonly used to avoid a divide-by-zero error.

blocks.code:
SELECT
  total_revenue / NULLIF(total_orders, 0) AS avg_order_value
FROM sales_summary;
-- If total_orders is 0, NULLIF returns NULL instead of 0,
-- and dividing by NULL gives NULL instead of a divide-by-zero error

rows: Multi-branch conditional logic — an if/elseif/else for a query
Returns the first non-NULL argument — a default value fallback
Returns NULL if a equals b, otherwise returns a — often used to prevent divide-by-zero

toc.text: CASE — If/Else Logic in a Query
NULLIF — Turn a Specific Value Into NULL

docs.title: Transactions — ACID Properties and Isolation Levels
docs.meta_title: SQL Transactions — ACID and Isolation Levels | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: The theory behind BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK from the earlier TCL lesson — the four ACID guarantees, and how isolation levels trade consistency for speed.

blocks.html: The earlier TCL lesson covered the commands — BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT. This lesson covers what those commands are actually guaranteeing, and why a database offers several different levels of that guarantee.
Both updates succeed together, or neither does — this money-transfer example is the classic illustration of why transactions exist.

rows: A transaction's changes all happen, or none of them do — no partial transfer where money leaves one account but never arrives at the other
A transaction can only move the database from one valid state to another — every constraint (from the earlier lesson) still holds afterward
Concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted changes — covered in depth below
Once committed, a change survives — even a server crash immediately after doesn't lose it

blocks.html: Multiple transactions often run at the same time. Without isolation, one transaction could read another's half-finished changes — a "dirty read" — and make a decision based on data that's about to be rolled back.

rows: The default in most databases (e.g. PostgreSQL, SQL Server)
Dirty reads + non-repeatable reads (a row changing mid-transaction)
Every concurrency issue — transactions behave as if run one at a time

blocks.html: A higher isolation level isn't automatically the right choice — Serializable can cause more transactions to fail and need retrying under heavy concurrent load. Most applications are well-served by the database's default.
blocks.title: Common Mistake

docs.title: Branching Basics
docs.meta_title: Git Branching Basics | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Working on a new feature without touching the working project — creating, switching, and listing branches.

blocks.html: Every commit so far in this course happened on one line of history. A branch lets development split — trying a new feature, fixing a bug, or experimenting — without touching the working version until it's ready.
A new repository starts with one branch, conventionally named main (older projects sometimes use master) — the project's stable, working line of history.

blocks.code:
git branch feature-login
# Creates the branch, but doesn't switch to it yet

git switch feature-login
# or, the older equivalent still seen everywhere:
git checkout feature-login

blocks.text: Creating and Switching in One Step

blocks.code:
git switch -c feature-login
# or
git checkout -b feature-login

git branch
#   main
# * feature-login   <- the asterisk marks the current branch

blocks.html: Commits made while on feature-login only exist on that branch — switching back to main makes those changes disappear from view (not deleted, just not part of main's history) until the branch is merged, covered in the next lesson.

blocks.code:
git switch feature-login
# ... make changes, git add, git commit ...
git switch main
# The feature-login commits aren't visible here yet

# Safe delete — refuses if the branch has unmerged changes
git branch -d feature-login

# Force delete, even with unmerged changes
git branch -D feature-login

blocks.html: Creating a branch for every real change — even a small one — costs almost nothing and keeps main always in a working state. This habit alone prevents most of the "I broke everything" moments a beginner runs into.

docs.title: Relational Databases — Concepts and SQL vs. NoSQL
docs.meta_title: Relational Databases and SQL vs. NoSQL | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: What actually makes a database "relational," the real benefits and limitations of that model, and how it compares to a NoSQL database.

blocks.html: Every earlier lesson in this course used a relational database without stopping to define what that word means. This lesson is the conceptual grounding — worth reading even after the syntax is comfortable.

Data is organized into tables (formally called relations), each with a fixed set of columns, and rows related to each other through shared keys — the foreign keys from the earlier Data Constraints lesson are exactly this relationship mechanism in practice.

A Relational Database Management System is the software that stores, organizes, and lets a program query relational data — PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, and Oracle Database are all RDBMSes; SQL is the language nearly all of them use.

rows: Constraints (PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK) enforce correctness at the database level, not just in application code
Normalization (organizing data to avoid repeating the same information in multiple places) keeps updates consistent
SQL is broadly transferable between different RDBMSes, unlike most NoSQL query APIs
A transaction's ACID guarantees (from the earlier lesson) make the data trustworthy under concurrent use
Every row in a table must fit the same column structure — awkward for data that's naturally irregular
Splitting a relational database across many servers while keeping joins fast is a genuinely hard problem
A query touching many related tables can slow down significantly as data grows, without careful indexing

blocks.html: A NoSQL database (MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, and others) trades some of the relational model's guarantees for flexibility and easier horizontal scaling — commonly storing documents, key-value pairs, or graphs instead of fixed-schema tables.

rows: Does the data have a clear, stable structure?
No — it varies row to row
Do relationships between records matter a lot?
Yes — joins are a core tool
Less — data is often self-contained per document
Sometimes acceptable to relax for speed/scale
Does it need to scale to huge, distributed volume?
Harder, though modern RDBMSes have improved this
Often designed for this from the start

blocks.html: This site's MongoDB course covers the NoSQL side of this comparison in depth — worth a look once the relational model here feels solid, to see the same problems solved a genuinely different way.
blocks.title: Where to go next

docs.title: Query Optimization Techniques
docs.meta_title: SQL Query Optimization Techniques | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Practical habits that make a slow query fast — reading an EXPLAIN plan, indexing what actually gets filtered on, and rewriting subqueries as joins.

blocks.html: The earlier Beyond the Basics lesson introduced EXPLAIN and indexes briefly. This lesson is a fuller, practical set of techniques for actually making a slow query fast.
EXPLAIN shows how the database actually plans to run a query — which indexes it'll use, in what order it'll touch each table, and roughly how many rows it expects at each step.

blocks.code:
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42;

-- A "Seq Scan" (sequential scan) means it's reading every row —
-- usually a sign a useful index is missing on customer_id
-- An "Index Scan" means it found and used an index — the goal

blocks.html: An index speeds up finding rows by a column's value, at the cost of some extra storage and slightly slower writes. The columns worth indexing are the ones actually used to filter or join — not every column.

Indexing every column "just in case" backfires — each index slows down every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on that table, since the index itself needs updating too. Index what queries actually filter or join on, not everything.
blocks.title: Common Mistake

blocks.html:
• Join on indexed columns — an unindexed join column forces the database to scan one side of the join row by row.
  • Filter before joining where possible — a WHERE clause that reduces one table's rows before the join means less data to combine.
  • Join only the tables actually needed — an unnecessary JOIN still costs work even if its columns are never selected.
A subquery re-run for every row of the outer query (a correlated subquery, from the earlier Subqueries lesson) can often be rewritten as a JOIN, which the database can usually plan more efficiently.

blocks.code:
-- Slower — the subquery runs once per row of products
SELECT name FROM products p
WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.product_id = p.id) > 0;

-- Often faster — rewritten as a join
SELECT DISTINCT p.name
FROM products p
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id;

blocks.html: Requesting only the columns actually needed, instead of every column, reduces the data the database has to read and send — a small habit that adds up significantly on a large table.

rows: Avoids scanning every row to find a match
Avoids a row-by-row scan on one side of a join
Reduces how much data gets combined
Avoids re-running the same subquery once per outer row

docs.title: The useReducer Hook
docs.meta_title: The useReducer Hook | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: An alternative to useState for state that updates through well-defined actions — how it works, and when it's worth reaching for over useState.

blocks.html: The State and Updating State lessons covered useState for most component state. useReducer is an alternative, better suited to state that changes through several distinct, well-defined actions rather than one simple value.
A reducer is a function that takes the current state and an action, and returns the new state — the same pattern this course's array .reduce() examples use, just applied to component state.
dispatch is the only way to trigger a state change — a component never sets state directly, it describes what happened (the action) and lets the reducer decide the result.

rows: State is a single value or a few independent ones
Several pieces of state update together in response to the same events
Updates are simple — set this to that
The next state genuinely depends on the current state and which action fired
There's no shared logic between different updates
The same transition logic needs to be testable on its own, separate from the component

blocks.html: A reducer function has no dependency on React at all — it's a plain function taking state and an action, returning new state. That makes it trivial to unit test without rendering anything.

docs.title: Suspense and Code-Splitting with React.lazy
docs.meta_title: Suspense and Code-Splitting | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Loading a component only when it's actually needed with React.lazy, and showing a fallback while it loads with Suspense.

blocks.html: By default, a React app's entire JavaScript bundle downloads before anything renders — including code for parts of the app a visitor might never open. Code-splitting breaks the bundle into pieces loaded on demand, and Suspense is how React shows a fallback while a piece is still loading.

blocks.text: React.lazy — Loading a Component on Demand

blocks.html: Instead of a normal import, React.lazy takes a function that dynamically imports a component — that import only actually happens the first time the component is rendered.

blocks.code:
import { lazy } from 'react'

const SettingsPage = lazy(() => import('./SettingsPage'))

blocks.html: A lazily-loaded component needs a <Suspense> boundary somewhere above it — its fallback prop is what shows while the component's code is still downloading.

blocks.text: A Practical Use — Splitting by Route

blocks.html: The most common real use: pairing lazy-loaded components with React Router (from the earlier lesson), so a route's code only downloads when a visitor actually navigates to it.

blocks.text: One Suspense Boundary Can Cover Several Components

blocks.html: A single <Suspense> shows its fallback until every lazy component inside it has finished loading — useful for treating a group of related pieces as one loading unit rather than showing several separate spinners.

Suspense also has a newer, more advanced use — suspending on data fetching itself, not just lazy component loading — supported by some data-fetching libraries and React's own newer APIs. That deeper use is beyond this lesson's scope; code-splitting is the well-established, universally supported case.
blocks.title: Suspense goes further than this lesson covers

docs.title: Using TypeScript with React
docs.meta_title: Using TypeScript with React | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Typing component props, state, and events in a React component — the practical patterns, assuming basic TypeScript familiarity.

blocks.html: This lesson assumes basic TypeScript syntax is already familiar — types, interfaces, generics — and focuses specifically on the patterns unique to typing a React component. A .tsx file extension (instead of .jsx) is what tells the TypeScript compiler a file contains JSX.
React's built-in ReactNode type covers anything valid as JSX children — text, elements, fragments, or nothing at all.
TypeScript usually infers the type from the initial value — an explicit type argument is only needed when the initial value doesn't fully describe every state the variable can hold.
React provides typed versions of DOM events, prefixed with React. — event.target is then correctly typed too, instead of being any.

blocks.text: Typing useRef for a DOM Element

rows: An interface, destructured in the function's parameter
Usually inferred; use useState<T>() when the initial value doesn't cover every possible state

blocks.html: Most tooling that scaffolds a React project (including Vite) offers a TypeScript template out of the box — starting a new project with it from day one avoids retrofitting types onto existing JavaScript later.

docs.title: Where to Go Next
docs.meta_title: React: Where to Go Next | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: A look at TypeScript, testing, and full frameworks like Next.js — the natural next steps once core React feels comfortable.

blocks.html: This section has covered core React — components, props, state, hooks, and the tools around them. This closing lesson points toward what a real project usually adds on top.

Most production React code today is written in TypeScript rather than plain JavaScript — adding type declarations to props, state, and function signatures, catching a whole category of mistakes (a missing prop, a typo'd field name) before the code ever runs. This site's own JavaScript section doesn't cover TypeScript, and it's a large enough topic to deserve its own dedicated learning path once React itself feels comfortable — the official TypeScript docs are the best starting point.

React Testing Library (usually paired with a test runner like Vitest or Jest) is the standard tool for testing components — deliberately built around testing what a user actually sees and does, rather than a component's internal implementation details.

Everything in this section is "just React" — rendering in the browser, one page. Real production sites very often sit on top of a framework that adds server-side rendering, file-based routing, and image/font optimization:

rows: The most widely used React framework — server rendering, file-based routing, both fully static and dynamic pages in one project
Deeply built around web fundamentals — forms and data loading tied closely to standard HTTP
Ships zero JavaScript by default — React components hydrate only where a page actually needs interactivity

blocks.text: State Management, at a Larger Scale

blocks.html: Context (from the Context API lesson) covers a lot of real cases, but very large applications sometimes reach for a dedicated state management library — Redux, Zustand, and Jotai are the most common — when state genuinely needs to be shared and updated from many unrelated places across a big app.

This section can't track every detail of a library that keeps evolving. The official React documentation is the authoritative, always-current reference — worth bookmarking, and worth reaching for whenever you need something more exhaustive than a lesson here provides.
The fundamentals in this section — components, props, state, effects, and the rules around them — are the same whichever of these you reach for next.

docs.title: Authentication — Passwords and JWTs
docs.meta_title: Node.js Authentication with JWT | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Hashing passwords safely with bcrypt, and issuing and verifying a JSON Web Token so an Express route can tell who's making a request.

blocks.html: The REST API lesson mentioned that not just anyone should be able to delete a product — this lesson is how that's actually enforced: hashing passwords safely, and issuing a token that proves who's making a request on every request afterward.

bcrypt hashes a password with a random salt baked in — the same password hashed twice produces two different results, which is exactly what stops a stolen password database from being searchable with a precomputed table of common passwords.

blocks.text: JWTs — Proving Who's Making a Request

blocks.html: After a successful login, the server issues a JSON Web Token — a signed string the client sends back on every future request (usually in an Authorization header) instead of logging in again each time.

blocks.text: Verifying a Token on a Protected Route

blocks.html: This is exactly the middleware pattern from the earlier Middleware lesson — requireAuth runs before the route handler, and can block the request entirely before it reaches the actual logic.

rows: Turns a plain password into a safe, salted hash for storage
Checks a login attempt's password against the stored hash
Issues a signed token after a successful login
Confirms a token is genuine and not expired, on every protected request

blocks.html: JWT_SECRET must be a long, random, private value kept in an environment variable — never committed to the repo. Anyone who obtains it can forge a valid token for any user.
blocks.title: The one secret this whole system depends on

docs.title: Testing Node.js Applications
docs.meta_title: Testing Node.js Applications | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Writing automated tests with Node's own built-in test runner — no extra package required — plus testing an Express route.

blocks.html: Node ships its own test runner built in — node:test — so a first real test needs no extra package at all. (Popular external runners like Jest and Vitest add extra features on top of the same core idea, worth exploring later.)

blocks.code:
node --test
# ✔ add() sums two numbers

blocks.html: Rather than starting a real server on a real port, a request library that can call an Express app directly (like supertest) tests routes without any network involved.

rows: a and b have the same structure/values (for objects and arrays)
An async function's returned promise rejects

blocks.html: A test suite that only ever exercises the "happy path" (valid input, success case) misses most real bugs — deliberately write at least one test for what should happen with bad input, a missing field, or an error thrown deep in the code.
blocks.title: Test the failure cases too

docs.title: Logging in Production
docs.meta_title: Logging in Node.js Production Apps | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Why console.log stops being enough once an app is actually running on a server, and the structured logging pattern that replaces it.

blocks.html: console.log works fine on a local machine, but a real running server needs more: log levels, timestamps, and output that can actually be searched later — usually across thousands of lines a day.

rows: An error and a routine info message look identical
Impossible to know when something happened after the fact
Hard to search or filter at scale — structured (JSON) logs can be queried
A real logger can be configured to skip verbose logs outside development

blocks.code:
import winston from 'winston'

const logger = winston.createLogger({
  level: 'info',
  format: winston.format.json(),
  transports: [new winston.transports.Console()],
})

logger.info('Server started', { port: 3000 })
logger.error('Database connection failed', { error: err.message })
{"level":"info","message":"Server started","port":3000,"timestamp":"2026-09-03T10:00:00.000Z"}

rows: Something unexpected, but the app kept working
Normal, notable events — a server starting, a user signing up
Detailed information, usually only enabled during active troubleshooting

blocks.html: morgan is Express-specific middleware (from the earlier Middleware lesson) that automatically logs every incoming request.

Never log a password, a full credit card number, or an API secret — even at the debug level. A log file is often less carefully protected than the database itself, and logs frequently get shipped to third-party monitoring tools.
blocks.title: What never belongs in a log

docs.title: Concurrency Beyond the Event Loop — Child Processes, Worker Threads, and Cluster
docs.meta_title: Node.js Concurrency — Child Process, Worker Threads, Cluster | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Three ways Node uses more than its one main thread — running another program, offloading CPU-heavy work, and using every CPU core for a server.

blocks.html: The earlier Event Loop lesson explained why Node handles many requests on a single thread — that works well because most server work is waiting (on a file, a database, a network response), not computing. These three tools cover the cases where that single thread genuinely isn't enough.
Runs a separate operating-system process — another program entirely, not more JavaScript on the same thread.

• Common uses: running a shell command, converting a file with an external tool (like ImageMagick or ffmpeg), or spawning another script.
  • The new process runs fully independently — Node's own event loop stays free while it works.

Unlike child_process, a worker thread runs more JavaScript, in a real OS thread separate from the main one — for CPU-intensive work (heavy computation, image processing, large data transformation) that would otherwise block the event loop for everyone.

Running heavy synchronous computation directly on the main thread (instead of a worker) blocks every request the server is handling — this is the actual failure mode "Node is single-threaded" warnings are about.
blocks.title: What worker_threads actually prevents

blocks.html: A single Node process only ever uses one CPU core. cluster forks multiple copies of the whole application — one per core — with a built-in load balancer distributing incoming requests between them.

rows: A separate OS process, any program
Running a shell command or external tool
More JavaScript, a separate OS thread
CPU-heavy computation that would block the event loop
Multiple copies of the whole app, one per CPU core
Using every core on a multi-core server for more throughput

blocks.html: Tools like PM2 (covered in this site's Hosting & Deployment course) manage clustering and process restarts automatically — worth knowing the underlying cluster module conceptually, even when a tool handles it in practice.
blocks.title: What most real projects actually use

docs.title: Making HTTP Requests from Node.js
docs.meta_title: Making HTTP Requests from Node.js | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Calling another API from a Node script or server using the built-in global fetch — no dependency required, GET and POST requests, and error handling.

blocks.html: Every earlier lesson in this course built a server that receives requests. This lesson is the other direction — a Node script or server calling another API, using the same fetch function already familiar from browser JavaScript.
Node 18 and later ships a global fetch — no package to install, no import needed.
Unlike most Node error handling, fetch does not throw for a 404 or 500 response — only for a genuine network failure. The status needs an explicit check.

Third-party libraries like axios still add real conveniences (automatic JSON parsing, request/response interceptors, built-in timeout handling) — worth reaching for on a larger project. Built-in fetch is enough for most everyday cases without adding a dependency.
blocks.title: When a library still helps

docs.title: Garbage Collection and Memory Leaks in Node.js
docs.meta_title: Node.js Garbage Collection and Memory Leaks | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: How Node frees memory automatically, and the Node-specific patterns — a growing cache, a forgotten listener, a global array — that quietly prevent it from doing so.

blocks.html: Node uses the same V8 JavaScript engine as Chrome, and the same automatic memory management from the earlier JavaScript course's Memory Management lesson — memory is freed once nothing references it anymore. A long-running server makes a leak's consequences far more visible than a browser tab ever does.

blocks.text: Why This Matters More on a Server

blocks.html: A browser tab gets closed and its memory reclaimed completely, often within minutes. A Node server is meant to run for days or weeks — a slow leak that's invisible in a five-minute test becomes a crash from running out of memory after enough traffic.

blocks.text: A Common Leak — an Ever-Growing Cache
A Common Leak — Event Listeners That Are Never Removed

blocks.html: Node prints a warning after 10 listeners accumulate on the same event by default — a "MaxListenersExceededWarning" in the console is a strong hint a listener is being added somewhere it's never being removed.
blocks.title: A built-in early warning

blocks.code:
node --inspect server.js
# Then open chrome://inspect in Chrome to attach DevTools —
# the Memory tab can take a heap snapshot, the same tool used
# for browser-side leak hunting in the earlier JavaScript lesson

rows: An unbounded cache (a plain object or Map that only grows)
Use an actual cache with a size limit and eviction (LRU)
Event listeners added repeatedly, never removed
Call .removeListener() / .off() when done, or use .once() for a one-time listener
A module-level array or object that keeps accumulating
Clear or bound it explicitly, or scope it to a request instead of the module
Store the interval ID and clearInterval() it when no longer needed
