docs.title: process.nextTick and setImmediate
docs.meta_title: process.nextTick and setImmediate in Node.js | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Two Node-specific ways to schedule a callback for "as soon as possible" — how they differ from each other and from setTimeout, and the exact order they run in.

blocks.html: The earlier Event Loop lesson covered the general model — the call stack, the task queue. Node adds two more specific scheduling tools on top of that model, both meaning roughly "run this very soon," but not identically.
A callback passed to process.nextTick runs immediately after the current operation finishes, before the event loop continues to anything else — even before promise callbacks.

blocks.code:
console.log('1')
process.nextTick(() => console.log('2 — nextTick'))
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3 — promise'))
console.log('4')

// Output: 1, 4, 2, 3 — nextTick runs before the promise microtask

blocks.html: Scheduled to run in a specific later phase of the event loop, after I/O callbacks (like a completed file read) for that cycle have run.

rows: Immediately after the current operation — before anything else, including promises
After nextTick callbacks, still before the event loop moves on
In the "check" phase of the event loop, typically after I/O callbacks
In the timers phase — similar timing to setImmediate, but not guaranteed to be first

blocks.html: Calling process.nextTick recursively without a stopping condition starves the entire event loop — nothing else (not I/O, not timers) ever gets a turn, since nextTick callbacks are drained completely before anything else runs.
blocks.title: A real footgun with process.nextTick

blocks.html:
• process.nextTick: ensuring a callback runs after the current synchronous code finishes, but strictly before any I/O or timer — used carefully, and rarely needed in typical application code.
  • setImmediate: deferring work until after pending I/O has been handled, so it doesn't delay something more time-sensitive.

docs.title: Template Engines — Server-Rendered HTML with EJS
docs.meta_title: Node.js Template Engines — EJS | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Rendering HTML on the server with data plugged in, using EJS with Express — for a page that's a traditional server-rendered site rather than an API or a React frontend.

blocks.html: Every earlier lesson in this course either returned JSON (a REST API) or assumed a separate frontend. A template engine is the traditional alternative — the server renders complete HTML pages directly, with data plugged into placeholders.

blocks.code:
import express from 'express'
const app = express()

app.set('view engine', 'ejs')
app.set('views', './views')   // where template files live

Welcome, <%= user.name %>!

Email: <%= user.email %>

blocks.html: <%= value %> outputs a value, automatically escaped for safety (the same escaping concept as the earlier Cybersecurity course's XSS-prevention lesson) — plain text stays plain text even if it contains HTML-looking characters.

blocks.text: Loops and Conditionals in a Template

blocks.code:
<% products.forEach(function(product) { %>
  • <%= product.name %> — $<%= product.price %>
    • <% }) %>
<% if (user.isAdmin) { %> Admin Panel <% } %>

blocks.html: <% ... %> (no =) runs JavaScript logic without outputting anything directly — loops and conditionals use this form.

blocks.code:
My Site

<%- include('partials/header') %>

Profile

blocks.html: <%- %> (with a dash) outputs raw, unescaped HTML — needed for include() since a partial's own HTML shouldn't be escaped away.

rows: Output raw HTML, not escaped (used for includes)

blocks.html: EJS is one option among several (Pug and Handlebars are common alternatives) — the underlying concept (server-rendered HTML with data plugged in) is the same across all of them, this lesson's syntax is EJS-specific.
blocks.title: One of several template engines

docs.title: Where This Leaves You
docs.meta_title: Node.js — Where This Leaves You | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: A recap of the Node.js course, and the practical next step: putting a routing, middleware, and database knowledge together into one real project.

blocks.html: This course took JavaScript out of the browser entirely and put it on the server: reading and writing files, listening for network requests, and eventually a complete REST API talking to a real database. Here's how the pieces fit together.

blocks.text: The Shape of What You Learned

blocks.html: Everything in this course builds toward one idea: a server that receives a request and decides how to respond. http showed the raw mechanism; Express made it practical with routing and middleware; the event loop explained why Node can do this for many visitors at once without slowing down; and streams, buffers, and the file system module gave you the tools to move data around efficiently while it happens.

blocks.text: How This Connects to the Rest of the Site

rows: Every function, array method, and async pattern from that course works identically in Node — nothing about the language itself changes
The full syntax for the queries this course's pool.query() calls send
A React frontend is exactly the kind of client that talks to the REST API built in this course

blocks.html: The most useful thing to do with everything in this course is combine it into one small, real project — a to-do list API, a simple blog backend, a guestbook — with actual routes, a real database, and a frontend (even a simple HTML page) that talks to it. Reading about routing and building it yourself surface completely different problems; the second kind is where this actually sinks in.

Node.js has a large ecosystem beyond what fits in an introductory course — testing frameworks, real-time communication with WebSockets, authentication libraries, deployment platforms. Everything here is the foundation those all sit on top of; comfortable with this, the rest is far more approachable than it looks from the outside.

docs.title: Decorators
docs.meta_title: Python Decorators | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: A function that wraps another function to add behavior without changing its code — the @ syntax, and why it's used constantly in real Python.

blocks.html: The earlier OOP lesson used @property without explaining the mechanism behind it. A decorator is a function that takes another function, wraps it with extra behavior, and returns the wrapped version — the @ syntax is just a convenient way to apply one.
@shout above def greet(): is exactly equivalent to writing greet = shout(greet) right after defining it.
A real decorator needs to pass through whatever arguments the wrapped function actually takes, without knowing them in advance.

rows: Lets a method be accessed like an attribute — covered in the earlier OOP lesson
Marks a method that doesn't use self at all
Passes the class itself (cls) instead of an instance
Caches a function's return value for repeated calls with the same arguments

blocks.html: A decorator is one of the cleanest ways to add cross-cutting behavior — logging, timing, caching, access checks — without repeating that logic inside every function it applies to.
blocks.title: Why this pattern is everywhere in real code

docs.title: Context Managers — the with Statement
docs.meta_title: Python Context Managers | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: The pattern behind "with open(...) as f" — guaranteed setup and cleanup, and how to write a context manager of your own.

blocks.html: The earlier File Handling lesson used with open('file.txt') as f: without explaining why. A context manager guarantees a cleanup step runs — closing a file, releasing a lock, closing a database connection — even if an error happens in between.

blocks.code:
with open('notes.txt') as f:
    content = f.read()
# f.close() runs automatically here — even if the code above raised an error

blocks.html: Without with, the same safety needs a manual try/finally — the whole point of a context manager is not needing to write that by hand every time.

blocks.code:
# The manual equivalent, for comparison
f = open('notes.txt')
try:
    content = f.read()
finally:
    f.close()

blocks.html: Any class implementing these two methods can be used with with.

blocks.code:
class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        import time
        self.start = time.time()
        return self

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_value, traceback):
        import time
        print(f'Elapsed: {time.time() - self.start:.2f}s')

with Timer():
    slow_operation()
# The elapsed time prints automatically when the block ends

blocks.html: For a simple case, a generator function decorated with @contextmanager avoids writing a whole class.

blocks.code:
from contextlib import contextmanager
import time

@contextmanager
def timer():
    start = time.time()
    yield
    print(f'Elapsed: {time.time() - start:.2f}s')

with timer():
    slow_operation()

blocks.html: Everything before yield runs as setup (like __enter__); everything after runs as cleanup (like __exit__), and always runs even if the block raises.

__exit__ receiving exception details (exc_type, exc_value, traceback) lets a context manager react to — or even suppress — an error, not just clean up after a successful block. Most simple context managers ignore these and just do cleanup regardless.
blocks.title: What those three __exit__ arguments are for

docs.title: Regular Expressions
docs.meta_title: Python Regular Expressions | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Pattern matching in text with the re module — searching, matching, and replacing text that follows a shape rather than an exact string.

blocks.html: A regular expression (regex) describes a pattern of text rather than an exact string — matching "any email address" or "any phone number," not one specific value. Python's built-in re module handles all of it.

blocks.code:
import re

text = 'My phone number is 555-1234'
match = re.search(r'\d{3}-\d{4}', text)

if match:
    print(match.group())   # 555-1234

rows: Zero or more of the previous character
One or more of the previous character
Zero or one of the previous character (optional)
Start of string / end of string

blocks.code:
text = 'Contact us at sam@example.com or admin@test.org'
emails = re.findall(r'[\w.]+@[\w.]+', text)
print(emails)   # ['sam@example.com', 'admin@test.org']

text = 'Call 555-1234 or 555-5678'
masked = re.sub(r'\d{3}-\d{4}', 'XXX-XXXX', text)
print(masked)   # Call XXX-XXXX or XXX-XXXX

blocks.html: Parentheses mark a part of the match worth pulling out separately.

blocks.code:
match = re.search(r'(\w+)@(\w+)\.com', 'sam@example.com')
print(match.group(1))   # sam
print(match.group(2))   # example

rows: Finds the first match anywhere in the string
Checks only at the very start of the string
Returns every match as a list
Replaces every match with new text
Splits a string wherever the pattern matches

blocks.html: A regex that becomes genuinely unreadable is a sign to reconsider it — a few named steps of plain string methods, or a dedicated parsing library for something structured like HTML, is often the better choice for complex cases.
blocks.title: When not to reach for regex

docs.title: Recursion
docs.meta_title: Python Recursion | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: A function calling itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem — the base case, the call stack it builds, and Python's recursion limit.

blocks.html: Recursion is a function solving a problem by calling itself with a smaller version of that same problem, until it reaches a version simple enough to answer directly.

blocks.text: The Base Case Is Not Optional

blocks.code:
def count_down(n):
    # Missing base case — this never stops on its own
    print(n)
    count_down(n - 1)
# count_down(5) eventually raises:
# RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded

blocks.html: Every recursive function needs a base case that's actually reachable — a base case that never triggers fails exactly the same way as no base case at all.
blocks.title: The most common recursion bug

blocks.html: Unlike some languages, Python enforces a default limit (usually 1000) on how deep a recursive call chain can go, specifically to catch runaway recursion before it crashes the interpreter.

blocks.code:
import sys
print(sys.getrecursionlimit())   # 1000, by default

# Raising it is possible but rarely the right fix —
# it usually means the problem should be solved with a loop instead
sys.setrecursionlimit(3000)

rows: Often reads more naturally for a naturally recursive problem (traversing a tree, nested data)
Usually faster and uses less memory for a simple repeated task
Each call adds a call stack frame — deep recursion can hit Python's recursion limit
No stack depth concern regardless of how many iterations

blocks.html: The Fibonacci example above recalculates the same values repeatedly — genuinely slow past small inputs. The earlier @functools.lru_cache decorator (from the Decorators lesson) fixes this specific problem by caching each result the first time it's computed.
blocks.title: A real optimization for recursive functions

toc.text: The Base Case Is Not Optional

docs.title: Concurrency — Threading, asyncio, and the GIL
docs.meta_title: Python Concurrency — Threading and asyncio | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Why Python's Global Interpreter Lock changes how concurrency works, and the two main tools — threading for I/O-bound waiting, asyncio for many concurrent tasks on one thread.

blocks.html: Doing more than one thing "at once" in Python is shaped by one specific detail most other languages don't have: the GIL.

blocks.text: The GIL — the Global Interpreter Lock

blocks.html: The GIL allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, even on a multi-core machine — a genuine limitation for CPU-heavy work split across threads, but far less of one for work that spends most of its time waiting (a network request, a file read), since the GIL is released during that wait.

blocks.code:
import threading
import time

def download(name):
    print(f'Starting {name}')
    time.sleep(2)   # stands in for a slow network request
    print(f'Finished {name}')

threads = [threading.Thread(target=download, args=(f'file{i}',)) for i in range(3)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()
# All 3 "downloads" run concurrently — total time ~2s, not ~6s

blocks.html: Because of the GIL, adding more threads does not speed up CPU-heavy computation (heavy math, image processing) — only genuinely I/O-bound waiting benefits. multiprocessing (separate processes, each with its own GIL) is the right tool for CPU-heavy parallelism, a topic beyond this lesson.
blocks.title: What threading does not fix

blocks.html: asyncio handles many waiting operations on a single thread, switching between them whenever one is waiting — no threads at all, similar in spirit to the event loop model from the JavaScript course.

blocks.code:
import asyncio

async def download(name):
    print(f'Starting {name}')
    await asyncio.sleep(2)
    print(f'Finished {name}')

async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(
        download('file1'),
        download('file2'),
        download('file3'),
    )

asyncio.run(main())
# Also ~2s total, no threads involved

blocks.html: async def marks a function as a coroutine — it can be paused at an await and resumed later, without blocking anything else. asyncio.gather() runs several coroutines concurrently and waits for all of them.

rows: Works with libraries that were never written with async in mind
Needs libraries built for it specifically (an async database driver, aiohttp instead of requests)
Real OS threads, some overhead per thread
Lighter weight — thousands of coroutines are practical, threads are not
Simpler to reason about for a handful of concurrent tasks
The standard modern choice for a server handling many concurrent connections

toc.text: The GIL — the Global Interpreter Lock

docs.title: Testing Python Code with unittest
docs.meta_title: Testing Python with unittest | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Writing automated tests with Python's own built-in unittest module — no extra package required — plus assert statements and test discovery.

blocks.html: Python ships its own testing framework built in — unittest — so a first real test needs no extra package at all. (pytest, mentioned in this site's Where to Go Next lesson, is a popular third-party alternative with a lighter syntax, worth exploring once the underlying ideas are comfortable.)

rows: A block of code raises the given exception

blocks.text: Testing That an Exception Is Raised

blocks.html: Run automatically before and after every test method in a class — useful for repeated preparation, like creating a fresh object each time.

blocks.text: Running Every Test in a Project

blocks.code:
python -m unittest discover
# Finds and runs every file matching test_*.py automatically

blocks.html: A test suite that only exercises the "happy path" (valid input, expected success) misses most real bugs — deliberately write at least one test for bad input, an edge case (an empty list, a zero), or an expected exception.
blocks.title: Test the failure cases too

Running Every Test in a Project

docs.title: Working with JSON
docs.meta_title: Python JSON Handling | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Converting a Python dict or list to JSON and back with the built-in json module — the standard format for a config file or an API response.

blocks.html: JSON is the standard format for exchanging data — an API response, a config file, data saved between program runs. Python's built-in json module handles converting between it and Python's own dicts and lists.

blocks.code: print(json.dumps(user, indent=2))

json_string = '{"name": "Sam", "age": 28}'
user = json.loads(json_string)
print(user['name'])   # Sam — a regular Python dict now

# Writing
with open('user.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(user, f, indent=2)

# Reading
with open('user.json') as f:
    user = json.load(f)

blocks.html: dump()/load() (no "s") work directly with an open file; dumps()/loads() (with an "s", for "string") work with a Python string already in memory.
A tuple converts to a JSON array and comes back as a Python list, not a tuple — JSON has no tuple type of its own, so that distinction is lost in the round trip.
blocks.title: A one-way conversion for tuples

docs.title: Virtual Environments
docs.meta_title: Python Virtual Environments | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Keeping each project's installed packages isolated from every other project's, using Python's own built-in venv module.

blocks.html: Installing a package with pip (from the earlier Modules and Imports lesson) normally installs it globally — shared across every Python project on the machine. A virtual environment gives one project its own isolated set of installed packages instead.
Project A needs version 1 of a library; Project B needs version 2 — installed globally, only one can be satisfied at a time. A virtual environment per project makes this a non-issue.
venv is built into Python — no separate install needed.

blocks.code:
python -m venv venv
# Creates a "venv" folder holding an isolated Python installation

# macOS / Linux
source venv/bin/activate

# Windows
venv\Scripts\activate

# The terminal prompt changes to show it's active, e.g.:
(venv) $

blocks.html: Once active, pip install only affects this environment — not the system-wide Python or any other project's environment.

blocks.code:
(venv) $ pip install requests
# Installed only inside this project's venv folder
(venv) $ deactivate

blocks.html: A requirements.txt file lists exactly what a project needs, so a teammate — or a deployment server — can recreate the same environment.

blocks.code:
# Save the current environment's packages to a file
pip freeze > requirements.txt

# On another machine, recreate it
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

rows: Activates it for the current terminal session

blocks.html: The venv folder itself should never be committed to version control — it's regenerated from requirements.txt on any machine. Add it to .gitignore from the start of a project.
blocks.title: What not to commit

docs.title: Type Hints in Depth
docs.meta_title: Python Type Hints | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Beyond a basic -> int — typing a list, an optional value, several possible types, and checking it all with mypy.

blocks.html: The earlier Functions lesson used a basic type hint like -> int. This lesson covers the fuller typing system — Python never enforces these at runtime on its own, but they document intent and let a separate tool catch real mistakes before the code even runs.

blocks.code:
def greet(name: str) -> str:
    return f'Hello, {name}!'

age: int = 28
price: float = 19.99
is_active: bool = True

blocks.text: Optional — a Value That Might Be None

blocks.code:
from typing import Optional

def find_user(user_id: int) -> Optional[str]:
    # Returns a username, or None if not found
    ...

# Python 3.10+ shorthand, no import needed:
def find_user(user_id: int) -> str | None:
    ...

blocks.text: Union — More Than One Possible Type

blocks.code:
def process(value: int | str) -> str:
    return str(value)

blocks.text: Typing a Function Passed as an Argument

blocks.html: Python itself never checks these hints while running — mypy, run separately, catches a mismatch before the code even executes.

blocks.code:
pip install mypy
mypy my_script.py
# my_script.py:5: error: Argument 1 to "greet" has incompatible type "int"; expected "str"

rows: A dict with string keys and integer values
Either an int or a string
A function taking an int and returning an int

blocks.html: Type hints are optional documentation, not enforcement — running the code with a "wrong" type still works fine unless something like mypy is run separately to check. Their value is catching a real class of bugs before runtime, and making a function's expected inputs obvious to anyone reading it.
blocks.title: What Python itself actually does with these

docs.title: Where to Go Next
docs.meta_title: Python: Where to Go Next | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Virtual environments and pip in practice, and a pointer to the frameworks and libraries built on top of core Python — Flask, Django, and pandas.

blocks.html: This section has covered core Python — the part that stays the same no matter which of the domains from the first lesson you go on to work in. This closing lesson covers one practical workflow habit, and points toward what comes next.

Different projects often need different, sometimes conflicting, versions of the same package. A virtual environment gives each project its own isolated set of installed packages, instead of one shared pile for your entire machine:

blocks.code:
python3 -m venv myproject-env      # create it, once per project
source myproject-env/bin/activate  # activate it (Windows: myproject-env\Scripts\activate)
pip install requests               # installs only into this project's environment
deactivate                          # done for now

blocks.html: Real Python projects create a virtual environment as one of the very first steps, before installing anything with pip. It's not a language feature, just a strong, near-universal convention — worth building the habit early.
blocks.title: Do this from your very first real project

rows: Flask (small, flexible) or Django (larger, more built-in structure)
The standard library alone often covers this — os, shutil, subprocess

blocks.html: None of these are covered in this section on purpose — each is substantial enough to deserve its own dedicated learning path once core Python feels comfortable, and picking one before you're ready to use it well tends to slow learning down rather than speed it up.

This section can't track every detail of a language that keeps evolving. The official Python documentation is the authoritative, always-current reference — worth bookmarking, and worth reaching for whenever you need something more exhaustive than a lesson here provides.

blocks.text: A Few Habits Worth Building Early

rows: Writing automated tests — catches a broken function before a user does
Automatic code formatting — one consistent style, no debate needed
Fast linting — flags unused imports, likely bugs, and style issues as you write

blocks.html: None of these are required to write working Python, and none are covered elsewhere in this section — they're mentioned here because real, professional Python codebases use all three routinely, and picking them up early is far cheaper than retrofitting them onto a large project later.
The fundamentals in this section — data types, control flow, functions, OOP, files, and databases — are the same whichever direction you take from here.

toc.text: A Few Habits Worth Building Early

docs.title: Array and Pattern Query Operators
docs.meta_title: MongoDB Array and Pattern Query Operators | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Querying inside an array field with $all, $elemMatch, and $size, and matching text patterns with $regex — extending the earlier Query Operators lesson.

blocks.html: The earlier Query Operators lesson covered comparison, logical, and element/existence operators. This lesson covers two more categories: matching inside array fields, and matching text by pattern rather than exact value.
Matches a document whose array field contains every value listed, in any order — unlike a plain array match, which requires an exact match of the whole array.
Needed when an array holds objects, and a single element must satisfy several conditions together — without it, conditions could each match a different element.

blocks.code:
db.products.find({ tags: { $size: 3 } })
// Matches only documents whose tags array has exactly 3 elements

blocks.html: $size only matches an exact length — there's no built-in $size: { $gt: 3 } for "more than 3." A common workaround is a separate stored count field, kept in sync when the array changes.
blocks.title: $size has no range version

blocks.html: Matches a string field against a regular expression, similar to the pattern matching from the earlier JavaScript course.

An unanchored $regex (no ^ at the start) can't use a text index efficiently and scans every document — fine on a small collection, worth watching on a large one. A dedicated text index (covered in the Specialized Indexes lesson) handles large-scale text search better.
blocks.title: A performance note

rows: An array containing every listed value
One array element satisfying multiple conditions together
An array with an exact number of elements

docs.title: Bulk Operations with bulkWrite()
docs.meta_title: MongoDB Bulk Operations — bulkWrite() | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Running many inserts, updates, and deletes in a single database round trip with bulkWrite(), instead of one operation at a time.

blocks.html: Each earlier lesson's insert, update, and delete operations run one at a time — fine for a handful of documents, but a real cost when hundreds or thousands need changing. bulkWrite() batches many operations into a single request to the database.
Each individual insertOne()/updateOne() call is its own round trip to the database server. bulkWrite() sends every operation together, cutting network overhead dramatically for a large batch.

blocks.code:
const result = db.products.bulkWrite([ /* ... */ ])
print(result.insertedCount)
print(result.modifiedCount)
print(result.deletedCount)

blocks.html: A common real use: importing a CSV or JSON file of thousands of records — read the file, build one bulkWrite() array of insertOne operations, and send it as a single batch instead of thousands of individual inserts.
blocks.title: The classic bulkWrite use case

docs.title: Multi-Document Transactions
docs.meta_title: MongoDB Multi-Document Transactions | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Making several writes across documents (or collections) succeed or fail together, and how read/write concerns tune the consistency guarantee.

blocks.html: A single updateOne() is always atomic on its own — it either fully applies or doesn't. A transaction extends that same all-or-nothing guarantee across several operations, possibly touching several documents or collections, the same concept as the earlier SQL course's transactions lesson.

blocks.text: Why This Matters — a Money Transfer Example

blocks.html: Moving money from one account to another needs two writes — subtract from one document, add to another. Without a transaction, a crash between the two writes leaves the data in a genuinely broken, inconsistent state.
Both updates commit together, or — if anything fails in between — neither one does, exactly like the earlier SQL transactions lesson's BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK.
MongoDB replicates data across multiple servers for durability — write concern and read concern tune how much of that replication a write or read waits for before being considered done.

rows: Acknowledgment from the primary server only
Acknowledgment from a majority of replica servers — safer, slightly slower
No acknowledgment at all — fastest, least safe

blocks.html: A transaction, by itself, only guarantees the writes inside it succeed or fail together — it says nothing about how durably they're replicated. For genuinely critical operations (like the money transfer above), pairing a transaction with a majority write concern is what most real applications actually use.
blocks.title: Transactions and write concern are separate guarantees

blocks.html: A transaction that touches many documents or runs for a long time can hurt performance across the whole database — reach for one specifically when an operation genuinely needs the all-or-nothing guarantee, not as a default habit for every multi-step write.
blocks.title: Not a default choice

toc.text: Why This Matters — a Money Transfer Example

docs.title: Specialized Indexes — Text, Geospatial, and TTL
docs.meta_title: MongoDB Specialized Indexes | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Three index types beyond single-field and compound — full-text search, location-based queries, and documents that automatically expire.

blocks.html: The earlier Indexes lesson covered single-field, compound, and unique indexes — all speeding up an exact or range match. These three types solve genuinely different problems.
Enables searching for words within a text field, rather than matching it exactly — the same kind of search a site's search bar typically needs.

A collection can only have one text index, though it can cover multiple fields at once (as above). For search needs beyond this — typo tolerance, weighted relevance tuning — MongoDB Atlas Search (mentioned in the PDF this lesson is based on) is the fuller tool; this covers the built-in basics.
blocks.title: The limits of a text index

blocks.html: Speeds up queries about location — finding everything within a distance of a point, or inside a boundary.

GeoJSON coordinates are [longitude, latitude] — the reverse of the [latitude, longitude] order many mapping APIs use. Swapping them silently produces a working query pointed at the wrong place on Earth.
blocks.title: A common ordering mistake

blocks.text: TTL Indexes — Documents That Expire Automatically

blocks.html: A TTL (Time To Live) index deletes a document automatically once a date field passes a set age — useful for session data, temporary tokens, or logs that shouldn't accumulate forever.

rows: Searching for words within a text field
Finding documents by location — nearby, within an area
Automatically deleting documents after a set time

toc.text: TTL Indexes — Documents That Expire Automatically

docs.title: Introduction to Version Control
docs.meta_title: Introduction to Version Control | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: What version control actually solves, why "final_v2_FINAL.docx" is the problem every developer eventually hits, and where Git fits in.

blocks.html: Anyone who has ever kept files named project_final.docx, project_final_v2.docx, and project_final_v2_ACTUAL.docx has already felt the exact problem version control solves — tracking how a project changes over time, without losing anything or guessing which copy is current.

rows: Multiple copies of a file, manually renamed
One file, a complete history of every change to it
No record of who changed what, or why
Every change is logged with an author, a timestamp, and a message
Undoing a mistake means finding an old copy, if one still exists
Undoing a mistake means checking out an earlier version — always possible
Two people editing the same file overwrite each other
Changes from multiple people merge together, with conflicts flagged explicitly

blocks.html: Early tools (like SVN and CVS) tracked changes with everyone working against one central copy — every action needed the network. Git, created by Linus Torvalds in 2005 to manage the Linux kernel's source code, is distributed instead: every developer has a complete copy of the project's full history on their own machine, and only needs the network to actually share changes with others.

These two names get used interchangeably, but they're different things. Git is the version control tool itself — it runs entirely on a local machine and has no concept of "the internet" built in. GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories online and adds collaboration features (pull requests, issues, code review) on top — covered starting a few lessons ahead. GitLab and Bitbucket, covered in the last lesson of this course, do the same job as GitHub with a different company behind them.

blocks.text: Why This Course Is Worth the Time

blocks.html: Every other course on this site assumes a project eventually gets deployed, shared, or worked on with someone else — Git is the tool that actually makes that possible without chaos. It's also, in practice, one of the first things a coding interview or a job's day-one setup assumes a developer already knows.

This course covers Git and GitHub in real depth, then closes with a lesson comparing GitHub to other hosting platforms (GitLab, Bitbucket) and other version control systems entirely (Mercurial, Subversion, Perforce) — Git is overwhelmingly the industry standard today, but it's worth knowing what else exists and why.
blocks.title: What "other version control softwares" means in this course

docs.title: Installing and Configuring Git
docs.meta_title: Installing and Configuring Git | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Getting Git installed on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and the one-time setup — your name and email — every commit will use.

blocks.html: Git runs entirely from the command line — the Windows Command Line and Linux Terminal lessons from the Cybersecurity course are directly useful preparation if either feels unfamiliar.

rows: Download and run the installer from git-scm.com — this also installs "Git Bash," a terminal that behaves like Linux's
Comes preinstalled on most systems, or run xcode-select --install, or install via Homebrew: brew install git

blocks.code:
git --version
# git version 2.43.0

blocks.html: Every commit records who made it — this needs to be set once, globally, before the first commit anywhere.

blocks.code:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

# Set the default branch name for new repositories to "main"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main

# Set a default text editor for commit messages (nano, here)
git config --global core.editor "nano"

# Make Git's output colorful in the terminal
git config --global color.ui auto

git config --list

# Check a single value
git config user.name

blocks.html: These settings are stored in a plain text file — ~/.gitconfig — and can be edited directly if preferred over running commands one at a time.
blocks.title: Where this actually lives

docs.title: Git Basics — init, add, commit
docs.meta_title: Git Basics — init, add, commit | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Turning a folder into a Git repository, and the two-step process — staging, then committing — behind every saved snapshot of a project.

blocks.html: Three commands cover the entire core loop of using Git day to day. Everything in the lessons ahead builds on these.

blocks.code:
mkdir my-project
cd my-project
git init
# Initialized empty Git repository in .../my-project/.git/

blocks.html: This creates a hidden .git folder — that's the entire repository. Deleting it removes all Git history while leaving the actual project files untouched.

blocks.text: The Three States a File Can Be In

rows: A file Git sees but hasn't been told to track yet, or a tracked file that has changed
A change marked as ready to be included in the next commit
A change permanently saved into the project's history

blocks.code:
echo "# My Project" > README.md

git add README.md      # stage one specific file
git add .               # stage every changed file in the current folder and below

git commit -m "Add README"
# [main (root-commit) a1b2c3d] Add README
#  1 file changed, 1 insertion(+)

blocks.html: The -m flag provides the commit message inline — without it, Git opens the configured text editor to write one.

blocks.code:
# 1. Make some changes to files
# 2. Check what changed (covered next lesson)
git status

# 3. Stage the changes
git add .

# 4. Commit them
git commit -m "Describe what changed and why"

blocks.html: A good commit message describes why a change was made, not just what — "Add README" is fine for a first commit, but "Fix off-by-one error in pagination" is far more useful six months later than "Fix bug."
blocks.title: Writing a useful commit message

toc.text: The Three States a File Can Be In

docs.title: Checking Status, Diffs, and History
docs.meta_title: Git Status, Diff, and Log | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: The three commands for seeing what changed, what will be committed, and what happened in the past — git status, git diff, and git log.

blocks.html: Before committing anything, it's worth actually seeing what's about to be saved — these three commands are how.

blocks.code:
git status
# On branch main
# Changes not staged for commit:
#   modified:   index.html
#
# Untracked files:
#   style.css

blocks.html: The single most-run Git command in practice — showing which files are modified, staged, or untracked, and what to do next.

blocks.code:
# See unstaged changes, line by line
git diff

# See staged changes (what's about to be committed)
git diff --staged

-

Old Heading

+

New Heading

blocks.html: A line starting with - was removed, + was added — the same convention used in the earlier PHP Security lesson's vulnerable/safe code comparisons.

blocks.code:
git log
# commit a1b2c3d4e5f6... (HEAD -> main)
# Author: Sam <sam@example.com>
# Date:   Wed Sep 3 10:00:00 2026
#
#     Add README

rows: One line per commit — a compact summary
The full diff for every commit, not just the message
Only commits by a specific person
Only commits that touched a specific file

blocks.code:
git log --oneline --graph
# * a1b2c3d Add README
# * e5f6g7h Initial commit

blocks.html: git log --oneline --graph is worth memorizing as a habit — it's the fastest way to see a project's recent history and branch structure at a glance, and becomes essential once branching (the next few lessons) is in the picture.
blocks.title: A command worth memorizing

docs.title: The .gitignore File
docs.meta_title: The .gitignore File | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Telling Git which files to never track — dependencies, secrets, and build output that don't belong in a repository's history.

blocks.html: Not every file in a project folder belongs in Git — installed dependencies, build output, and secrets should never be tracked. A .gitignore file tells Git which files or folders to ignore entirely.

blocks.code:
# .gitignore
node_modules/
.env
*.log
dist/
.DS_Store

rows: A specific folder, anywhere in the project
Only a build folder at the project root, not one nested deeper
An exception — un-ignores one specific file that would otherwise match a pattern above it
node_modules/, vendor/ — reinstalled from package.json/composer.json instead
.env — from the earlier PHP/Node lessons on environment variables
dist/, build/ — regenerated from source, not source itself

blocks.text: A File Already Tracked Won't Be Ignored Automatically

blocks.html: Adding a pattern to .gitignore only affects files Git doesn't already know about — a file already committed keeps being tracked until explicitly removed.

blocks.code:
# Stop tracking a file, but keep it on disk
git rm --cached .env
git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"

blocks.html: If a secret (an API key, a password) was ever committed, adding it to .gitignore afterward does NOT remove it from history — it's still recoverable from any earlier commit. Rotating the exposed secret immediately is the actual fix; removing it from history entirely is a separate, more advanced operation.
blocks.title: A leaked secret needs rotating, not just ignoring

toc.text: A File Already Tracked Won't Be Ignored Automatically

docs.title: Merging Branches
docs.meta_title: Git Merging Branches | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Bringing a branch's changes into another branch — fast-forward merges vs. a real merge commit, and reading what happened afterward.

blocks.html: Once work on a branch is ready, merging brings its changes into another branch — usually back into main.

blocks.code:
git switch main
git merge feature-login
# Updating a1b2c3d..e5f6g7h
# Fast-forward
#  login.php | 20 ++++++++++++++++++
#  1 file changed, 20 insertions(+)

blocks.html: The merge command runs on the branch receiving the changes (main, here), pulling in the named branch (feature-login).

blocks.text: Fast-Forward vs. a Real Merge Commit

rows: main hasn't changed since the branch split off
Both main and the branch have new commits since they split
Git simply moves main's pointer forward — no new commit created
Git creates a new commit specifically joining the two histories
A history showing exactly where branches diverged and rejoined

blocks.code:
# Force a real merge commit even when a fast-forward is possible —
# some teams prefer this for a clearer history of feature branches
git merge --no-ff feature-login

blocks.html: Once merged, a feature branch has usually done its job — deleting it keeps the branch list from growing indefinitely.

blocks.code: git branch -d feature-login

git log --oneline --graph --all
# *   f7g8h9i Merge branch 'feature-login'
# |\
# | * e5f6g7h Add login validation
# | * d4e5f6g Add login form
# |/
# * a1b2c3d Initial commit

blocks.html: A merge that touches the same lines a branch and main both changed can't be resolved automatically — that's a merge conflict, covered in the next lesson, and it's a completely normal part of working with branches, not a sign something went wrong.
blocks.title: What happens next if this doesn't go cleanly

toc.text: Fast-Forward vs. a Real Merge Commit

docs.title: Resolving Merge Conflicts
docs.meta_title: Resolving Git Merge Conflicts | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: What a merge conflict actually is, reading Git's conflict markers, and the exact steps to resolve one and finish the merge.

blocks.html: A merge conflict happens when Git can't automatically combine two changes — usually because both branches edited the exact same lines differently. It's not an error to be afraid of; it's Git correctly refusing to guess.

blocks.code:
git merge feature-login
# Auto-merging index.html
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in index.html
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.

blocks.html: Git edits the conflicted file directly, marking both versions.

blocks.code:
Welcome

<<<<<<< HEAD

This is the main branch version.

=======

This is the feature-login branch version.

>>>>>>> feature-login

rows: Start of the current branch's version
End of the incoming branch's version, naming it

blocks.html: Edit the file by hand — keep one version, keep the other, or write something combining both — and remove every marker line entirely.

blocks.code:
Welcome

This is the main branch version.

git add index.html
git commit
# Git pre-fills a merge commit message — usually fine to accept as-is

# See every file still needing resolution
git status
# Both modified:   index.html
# Both modified:   style.css

blocks.html: If a merge goes badly wrong partway through, it can be abandoned completely, returning to the state right before it started.

blocks.code: git merge --abort

blocks.html: Most code editors (VS Code among them) show conflict markers with clickable "Accept Current," "Accept Incoming," and "Accept Both" buttons — genuinely worth using instead of editing markers by hand once conflicts happen regularly.
blocks.title: A faster way to resolve these in practice

docs.title: Undoing Changes — checkout, reset, revert
docs.meta_title: Undoing Changes in Git | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Three different ways to undo something in Git, each for a different situation — discarding an uncommitted edit, rewinding history, and safely undoing a shared commit.

blocks.html: Git offers several distinct ways to undo something — picking the right one depends on exactly what needs undoing, and whether it's already been shared with anyone else.

blocks.code:
# Discard changes to one file, back to the last commit
git checkout -- index.html
# or, the newer equivalent:
git restore index.html

blocks.html: This permanently discards the uncommitted change — there's no undo for an undo here. Worth double-checking git diff first to see exactly what would be lost.
blocks.title: This one is irreversible

blocks.code:
# Move a staged file back to just "modified" — the change itself is kept
git restore --staged index.html

blocks.html: Moves the current branch pointer backward, with three levels of how much gets undone along with it.

rows: The last commit is undone, but its changes stay staged
The last commit is undone, changes stay in the working folder but unstaged
The last commit AND its changes are both gone entirely

blocks.html: git reset --hard discards work with no recovery through normal means. Never run it without being certain — and never on a commit that's already been pushed and shared with others, covered below.
blocks.title: The most dangerous command in this lesson

blocks.text: git revert — Safely Undoing a Shared Commit

blocks.html: Rather than erasing a commit from history, revert creates a brand-new commit that undoes its changes — the original commit stays in history, which is exactly what's needed once a commit has already been pushed and others may have it.

blocks.code:
git revert a1b2c3d
# Creates a new commit that undoes commit a1b2c3d's changes

rows: An uncommitted change, not staged yet
A commit made locally, never pushed or shared
A commit already pushed and possibly shared with others
git revert — never reset a shared commit

toc.text: git revert — Safely Undoing a Shared Commit

docs.title: Stashing Changes
docs.meta_title: Git Stash | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Temporarily setting aside uncommitted work to switch branches cleanly, without committing something half-finished.

blocks.html: Switching branches with uncommitted changes in the way is a common snag — git stash temporarily shelves those changes without committing them, so a branch switch can happen cleanly.

blocks.code:
git status
# modified: index.html (not staged)

git stash
# Saved working directory and index state WIP on main: a1b2c3d Add README

git status
# nothing to commit, working tree clean

git stash pop
# Restores the most recent stash AND removes it from the stash list

# Restore it but keep the stash entry too, for applying elsewhere
git stash apply

git stash list
# stash@{0}: WIP on main: a1b2c3d Add README
# stash@{1}: WIP on feature-login: e5f6g7h Add form

git stash apply stash@{1}   # apply a specific one, not just the most recent
git stash push -m "Half-finished login validation"

blocks.html: A typical real use: mid-way through a change, an urgent bug needs fixing on main right now. git stash, switch to main, fix the bug, switch back, git stash pop — the half-finished work resumes exactly where it was left.
blocks.title: The classic use case

docs.title: Remotes — Clone, Push, Pull, and Fetch
docs.meta_title: Git Remotes — Clone, Push, Pull, Fetch | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Connecting a local repository to GitHub — downloading an existing project, sending local commits up, and getting others' commits back down.

blocks.html: A remote is a repository hosted elsewhere — usually on GitHub — that a local repository stays connected to.

blocks.text: git clone — Downloading an Existing Repository

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/username/repo-name.git
cd repo-name
# A complete copy, full history included, ready to work on

blocks.text: Connecting an Existing Local Repository to GitHub

blocks.html: For a project that started with git init locally, rather than a clone — create an empty repository on GitHub first, then connect it.

blocks.code:
git remote add origin https://github.com/username/repo-name.git
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main

blocks.html: origin is the conventional name for a repository's primary remote — not a special keyword, just the default everyone uses.

blocks.text: git push — Sending Local Commits Up

blocks.code:
git push
# Sends commits on the current branch to the remote

# First push of a new branch needs -u (short for --set-upstream)
# to link the local and remote branch together, once:
git push -u origin feature-login
# Every push after that, on that branch, can just be: git push

blocks.text: git pull — Getting Others' Commits Down

blocks.code:
git pull
# Downloads new commits from the remote and merges them into the current branch
# Equivalent to: git fetch, then git merge

blocks.html: Downloads what changed on the remote without touching local files — useful for seeing what's new before deciding whether to merge it in.

blocks.code:
git fetch
git log origin/main   # see what's new on the remote before pulling it in

git remote -v
# origin  https://github.com/username/repo-name.git (fetch)
# origin  https://github.com/username/repo-name.git (push)

docs.title: Git Workflows — Feature Branches and Commit Conventions
docs.meta_title: Git Workflows | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: How a real team actually uses everything from earlier lessons together — a feature branch workflow, and writing commits that stay useful months later.

blocks.html: Every command in this course so far is a building block. This lesson is how they combine into the habits a real team (or a disciplined solo developer) actually follows day to day.

rows: 2. Create a branch for one specific change
4. Push and open a pull request
5. Address review feedback with more commits
Same branch, more commits, pushed again
6. Merge once approved, then delete the branch
Usually done through GitHub's merge button
Maintenance work — dependency updates, config changes

blocks.html: A widely-used commit message format that makes a project's history scannable and machine-parseable (some tools auto-generate changelogs from it).

blocks.code:
feat: add password reset flow
fix: correct off-by-one error in pagination
docs: update README installation steps
refactor: simplify user validation logic
test: add coverage for edge cases in checkout
chore: bump dependency versions

blocks.html: One commit per logical change, not one commit per work session — a commit fixing a bug and a commit adding an unrelated feature should never be the same commit, even if they happened back to back.
A useful test for commit size: could this specific commit be reverted on its own, cleanly, without breaking something unrelated? If not, it's probably bundling more than one logical change.
blocks.title: A gut check for commit size

docs.title: Rebasing vs. Merging
docs.meta_title: Git Rebase vs Merge | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: A second way to bring a branch up to date — rewriting its history onto a new base instead of merging — and the one rule about never rebasing shared history.

blocks.html: The earlier Merging lesson covered one way to combine branches. Rebasing achieves a similar goal — bringing a branch up to date with another — through a genuinely different mechanism, with a different result.

Rather than creating a merge commit joining two histories, rebase replays a branch's commits one by one on top of another branch's latest commit — rewriting history as if the branch had been created from that newer point all along.

blocks.code:
git switch feature-login
git rebase main
# feature-login's commits are now replayed on top of main's latest commit

blocks.text: Merge vs. Rebase — the Resulting History

rows: Preserves exactly what happened, including a merge commit showing where branches joined
Rewrites history into a single clean, linear line — no merge commit
Changes every rebased commit's hash — they become new commits entirely
Safe on any branch, shared or not
Only safe on a branch nobody else has already pulled

blocks.text: The One Rule That Actually Matters

blocks.html: Never rebase a commit that's already been pushed and shared with anyone else. Rebase rewrites commit history — a teammate who already pulled the old commits ends up with a repository that looks like it diverged from everyone else's, and untangling it is genuinely painful. Rebase a local, unshared branch freely; never rebase main, or a branch someone else is also working on.
blocks.title: Never rebase shared history

blocks.text: A Common, Safe Use — Cleaning Up Before a Pull Request

blocks.code:
# Squash several small "wip" commits into fewer, meaningful ones,
# before opening a pull request — safe because the branch isn't shared yet
git rebase -i HEAD~5

blocks.text: Keeping a Branch Updated — Merge or Rebase?

rows: A shared branch, or already-pushed commits
A local, not-yet-pushed feature branch, wanting a clean history
git rebase main is a common, safe choice

docs.title: Creating a GitHub Repository
docs.meta_title: Creating a GitHub Repository | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Walking through GitHub's "Create a new repository" screen — naming, visibility, and the README/gitignore/license checkboxes.

blocks.html: Starting a repository on GitHub itself — rather than pushing a local one up, as the previous lesson covered — is the more common starting point for a brand-new project.
From the "+" menu at the top of any GitHub page, or the green "New" button on the repositories tab.

rows: Becomes part of the repo's URL — lowercase-with-dashes is the near-universal convention
Shows under the repo name everywhere it's listed — worth writing even if optional
Covered in the Introduction to GitHub lesson
Creates a starter README.md immediately — usually worth checking
GitHub offers a pre-built template for dozens of languages/frameworks — a fast start on the earlier .gitignore lesson's file
Only matters for a public repo meant to be reused by others — MIT is the common, permissive default

blocks.code:
git clone https://github.com/username/new-repo-name.git
cd new-repo-name
# Start working — the README/gitignore/license chosen above are already there

blocks.html: Checking "Add a README" and picking a .gitignore template when creating a repo through GitHub's own form saves the manual setup work the earlier lessons in this course did by hand — both approaches end up in the same place.
blocks.title: The fast path vs. the from-scratch path

blocks.caption: The real repository-creation form — this is what deciding a name, visibility, and starter files actually looks like.

docs.title: Other Version Control Systems and Git Hosts
docs.meta_title: Other Version Control Systems and Git Hosts | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps as GitHub alternatives, and older version control tools — Subversion, Mercurial, Perforce — still found in real projects.

blocks.html: Git is overwhelmingly the industry standard today, and GitHub the most widely used place to host it — but neither is the only option, and knowing what else exists helps make sense of an older codebase or a company using a different tool.

blocks.text: Other Places to Host a Git Repository

rows: The largest, most widely used — covered throughout this course
Strong built-in CI/CD pipelines; also offers a fully self-hosted version companies can run on their own servers
Tight integration with other Atlassian tools (Jira, Confluence) — common in teams already using those
Integrated into Microsoft's broader Azure DevOps suite, common in enterprise .NET shops
A minimal, text-first alternative favored by some open-source projects that prefer email-based patches over pull requests

blocks.html: All of these host Git repositories — everything from the earlier lessons (branches, commits, merges) works identically regardless of which one a project uses. The difference is entirely in the collaboration features layered on top (issues, CI/CD, project boards) and each platform's own interface.

blocks.text: Version Control Systems Other Than Git

rows: Centralized (not distributed like Git) — one central server holds the only full history
Some older enterprise codebases, particularly pre-2010 projects
Distributed, conceptually similar to Git, with a reputation for a simpler command set
Facebook's internal monorepo historically used it; some open-source projects still do
Centralized, built for very large binary files (game assets, video)
Common in game development and other industries with huge non-text files Git handles poorly
One of the earliest widely-used systems, largely superseded
Occasionally in genuinely old, unmaintained projects

blocks.html: Git's distributed model (every developer has the complete history, from the first lesson in this course) made branching and merging fast and cheap compared to the centralized tools that came before it — combined with GitHub's network effects, that's largely why Git become the default choice for the vast majority of new projects since around 2010.

None of these alternatives need to be learned in depth to work productively — the concepts from this entire course (commits, branches, merging, remotes) transfer directly, since Git borrowed and refined ideas that existed in some form in most of them.
blocks.title: The good news about all of this

docs.title: Forking and Pull Requests
docs.meta_title: GitHub Forking and Pull Requests | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Contributing to a project without direct write access — forking a repository, making changes, and opening a pull request for review.

blocks.html: A fork is a personal copy of someone else's repository, made on GitHub — the standard way to contribute to a project without needing direct write access to the original.

rows: Click "Fork" on the original repo — GitHub creates a full copy under your own account
git clone your-fork-url — work on it locally, just like any other repository
Create a branch for the change, commit as usual — the earlier branching lessons apply directly
git push — sends the commits to your copy, not the original
From GitHub, propose merging your fork's branch into the original repository

blocks.text: What a Pull Request Actually Is

blocks.html: A pull request (PR) is a request to merge one branch into another, with a diff view, a comment thread, and (often) automated checks — the review step before code becomes part of the main project.

rows: The description and every comment on the PR
Every individual commit included in the PR
A full diff of every file touched — the same +/- format from the earlier git diff lesson
Available once checks pass and (usually) a reviewer approves

blocks.html: The original repository keeps moving after a fork is made — pulling in its new changes keeps a fork from falling behind.

blocks.code:
git remote add upstream https://github.com/original-owner/repo-name.git
git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main

blocks.html: A pull request doesn't need to be "finished" before opening it — a draft PR, opened early with a clear note that it's a work in progress, is a completely normal and welcomed way to get early feedback on direction before investing more time.
blocks.title: Opening a PR early is fine

blocks.alt: A real, merged pull request on a public GitHub repository, showing the conversation, commits, and files-changed tabs
blocks.caption: A real merged pull request — the review step before code becomes part of a project.

toc.text: What a Pull Request Actually Is

docs.title: GitHub Issues and Project Boards
docs.meta_title: GitHub Issues and Project Boards | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Tracking bugs, feature requests, and tasks directly inside a GitHub repository — labels, assignees, linking issues to commits, and a lightweight project board.

blocks.html: An issue is a tracked item on a repository — a bug report, a feature request, or a task — living alongside the code itself rather than in a separate tool.
From a repository's Issues tab, "New issue" — a title, a description (Markdown supported, same as a README), and optional labels/assignee.

rows: Categorize — bug, enhancement, documentation, good first issue
Group issues toward a specific release or deadline
Discussion thread, same as a pull request's

blocks.text: Linking an Issue to a Commit or PR

blocks.html: A specific phrase in a commit message or pull request description automatically closes the referenced issue once merged.

blocks.code:
git commit -m "Fix login validation bug

Fixes #42"

rows: Links to the issue without closing it

blocks.html: GitHub Projects turns a repository's issues into a Kanban-style board (To Do / In Progress / Done) — genuinely useful for a small team or a solo developer planning work, without needing a separate tool like Trello.

Issues labeled "good first issue" on a real open-source project are specifically curated to be approachable for a first-time contributor — a practical, low-stakes way to practice the fork-and-pull-request workflow from the previous lesson on a real codebase.

docs.meta_description: A closing summary of this course, and how Git connects directly to the Hosting & Deployment and Career Skills courses elsewhere on this site.

rows: Commit in small, logical steps with a clear message

blocks.text: A Few Things Worth Knowing Exist, Not Covered Here

rows: Git hooks (running a script automatically on commit/push)
A genuinely advanced customization, rarely needed starting out
A niche need, and a famously confusing feature even for experienced developers
A real, valuable topic, but its own course-worth of material — CI/CD generally
Security-hardening territory, rarely needed for a student or freelancer's day-to-day

blocks.html: The single most valuable next step: pick a real project — even a small personal one — put it on GitHub, and use everything from this course on it for a few weeks. Reading about branching is nothing like the moment a real merge conflict actually happens and gets resolved.

docs.meta_title: GitHub README and Markdown | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: The Markdown syntax GitHub renders everywhere — headings, code blocks, links, images — and what actually belongs in a project's README.

blocks.html: A README.md is usually the first — sometimes the only — thing anyone sees about a project. GitHub renders it as formatted text automatically, using Markdown, a lightweight syntax used everywhere on the platform (issues, pull requests, comments too).

blocks.code:
# Heading 1
## Heading 2
### Heading 3

**bold text**
*italic text*

- Bullet point
- Another one

1. Numbered item
2. Another one

[Link text](https://example.com)
![Image alt text](image.png)

`inline code`

```javascript

```

> A blockquote

| Column 1 | Column 2 |
|----------|----------|

blocks.text: What a Good README Actually Includes

rows: Project title and a one-line description
What this is, in five seconds
The exact commands to get it running locally
A code snippet or screenshot showing it in action
A live demo link, if there is one
The fastest way to actually see it work
Whether and how others can use the code — from the earlier repository-creation lesson

blocks.code:
# Todo App

A simple todo list built with vanilla JavaScript.

## Setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/username/todo-app.git
cd todo-app
open index.html
```

## Features

- Add and remove tasks
- Mark tasks complete
- Saves to localStorage

## License

MIT

blocks.html: A README written for a stranger who knows nothing about the project — not a note-to-self — is the right target. If a new visitor can't tell what the project does and how to run it within the first few lines, the README needs work regardless of how good the code is.

docs.title: HEAD and Detached HEAD
docs.meta_title: Git HEAD and Detached HEAD | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: What HEAD actually points to — the concept behind the conflict markers, resets, and checkouts from earlier lessons — and what "detached HEAD" means.

blocks.html: HEAD has appeared several times already — the earlier Merge Conflicts lesson's <<<<<<< HEAD marker, and git reset --soft HEAD~1 from Undoing Changes. This lesson explains what it actually is.

blocks.text: HEAD Is a Pointer to "Right Now"

blocks.html: HEAD points to whatever commit is currently checked out — normally, that means it points to the tip of the current branch, which itself points to the latest commit.

blocks.code:
cat .git/HEAD
# ref: refs/heads/main

# HEAD -> main -> the latest commit on main

blocks.text: Referring to Commits Relative to HEAD

rows: The direct parent of HEAD — equivalent to HEAD~1 for a normal commit

blocks.text: Detached HEAD — Checking Out a Specific Commit

blocks.html: Normally HEAD points to a branch. Checking out a specific commit directly (rather than a branch name) detaches HEAD from any branch — it now points straight at that one commit instead.

blocks.code:
git checkout a1b2c3d
# Note: switching to 'a1b2c3d'.
# You are in 'detached HEAD' state...

blocks.html: Looking around in detached HEAD state — checking old file contents, testing something — is completely safe. The risk is committing new changes while detached: those commits exist, but aren't on any branch, and become genuinely hard to find again once something else is checked out.

A commit made in detached HEAD state, with no branch pointing to it, can effectively be lost once HEAD moves elsewhere — Git eventually garbage-collects commits nothing references. To keep work made in this state, create a branch from it before switching away.
blocks.title: The real risk of detached HEAD

blocks.code:
# If changes made in detached HEAD are worth keeping, save them to a branch first:
git switch -c rescue-branch

# Otherwise, just return to a normal branch:
git switch main

toc.text: HEAD Is a Pointer to "Right Now"
Referring to Commits Relative to HEAD
Detached HEAD — Checking Out a Specific Commit

docs.title: Cherry-Picking and Amending Commits
docs.meta_title: Git Cherry-Pick and Commit --amend | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Copying one specific commit onto another branch, and fixing the very last commit's message or contents without creating a new one.

blocks.html: Two small, frequently useful commands for handling commits individually, rather than through a full merge or rebase.

blocks.text: git cherry-pick — Copying One Specific Commit

blocks.html: Applies a single commit from anywhere in the project's history onto the current branch — useful when exactly one fix or change is needed from another branch, not everything on it.

blocks.code:
git switch main
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d
# Applies commit a1b2c3d's exact changes as a new commit on main

blocks.html: A real use: a bug fix committed on a feature branch also needs to go out immediately on main, without merging the feature branch's unfinished work along with it.

Just like a merge, a cherry-pick can conflict if the target branch has diverged too much — resolved exactly the same way as the earlier Merge Conflicts lesson: edit the file, remove the markers, then continue.

blocks.code:
# After resolving conflict markers in the affected files:
git add .
git cherry-pick --continue

# Or abandon the cherry-pick entirely:
git cherry-pick --abort

blocks.text: git commit --amend — Fixing the Last Commit

blocks.html: Rather than creating a new commit for a typo or a forgotten file, --amend folds a change into the most recent commit instead.

blocks.code:
# Fix just the commit message
git commit --amend -m "Corrected commit message"

# Add a forgotten file to the last commit, keeping the same message
git add forgotten-file.txt
git commit --amend --no-edit

blocks.html: --amend rewrites the last commit entirely — it gets a new hash. Exactly the same rule as reset and rebase from earlier lessons: never amend a commit that's already been pushed and possibly pulled by someone else.
blocks.title: The same shared-history rule applies here

rows: Copying one specific commit onto the current branch
Fixing the message or contents of the most recent, not-yet-shared commit

toc.text: git cherry-pick — Copying One Specific Commit
git commit --amend — Fixing the Last Commit

docs.title: Tagging and GitHub Releases
docs.meta_title: Git Tagging and GitHub Releases | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: Marking a specific commit as a version — v1.0.0 — with a Git tag, and turning that into a downloadable GitHub Release with notes.

blocks.html: A tag marks one specific commit permanently — most commonly to record a release version, so "v1.0.0" always points to the exact commit that was actually shipped.

blocks.code:
# A lightweight tag — just a name pointing to a commit
git tag v1.0.0

# An annotated tag — includes a message, author, and date (recommended for releases)
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "First stable release"

git tag
# v1.0.0

git show v1.0.0
# Shows the tag's message and the commit it points to

blocks.html: Tags aren't included in a normal git push — they need to be pushed explicitly.

blocks.code:
git push origin v1.0.0

# Push every tag at once
git push origin --tags

git checkout v1.0.0
# Same detached HEAD situation as checking out any specific commit —
# from the earlier HEAD lesson

blocks.text: Turning a Tag into a GitHub Release

blocks.html: On GitHub, a Release is a tag with release notes, and optionally downloadable files attached (a compiled binary, a build artifact) — created from a repository's "Releases" section, usually based on an existing tag.

rows: Just a name pointing to a commit
A tag, plus formatted release notes and optional file attachments
Works with any Git host, or no host at all
A GitHub-specific feature built on top of tags
Created through GitHub's web interface or gh CLI

docs.title: Command Line and Terminal Basics
docs.meta_title: Command Line and Terminal Basics | Learn Computer Academy
docs.meta_description: What a terminal actually is, why developers use it instead of clicking, and the handful of navigation commands you'll use in every session.

blocks.html: Almost every real developer tool — installing packages, running a script, using Git — happens through typed commands, not clicked icons. The terminal (also called the command line or console) is where you type them.

A normal app is a GUI — a Graphical User Interface — where you click buttons and icons. A terminal is a CLI — a Command-Line Interface — where you type a line of text describing exactly what you want done, and the computer does it immediately, with no menus in between.

On Windows, search for PowerShell or Windows Terminal in the Start menu. On macOS, open the Terminal app from Applications → Utilities. Both give you the same kind of typing-based window — the exact commands differ slightly, which is exactly why the table below shows both.

blocks.alt: Isometric diagram of a computer terminal window with a command-line cursor, with arrows flowing from the window down to a stack of file icons representing files being controlled by typed commands
blocks.caption: Every command you type in a terminal acts directly on your file system — no clicking or menus involved.

blocks.code:
PS C:\Users\Rahul> cd projects
PS C:\Users\Rahul\projects> dir
my-site   notes.txt
PS C:\Users\Rahul\projects> cd my-site
PS C:\Users\Rahul\projects\my-site>

blocks.html: Press the ↑ arrow to bring back your last command instead of retyping it, and press Tab to auto-complete a file or folder name — both work in every terminal you'll ever use.
blocks.title: Two habits worth building immediately

blocks.text: Creating and Removing Files and Folders

blocks.html: Navigation gets you around; these commands let you actually change what's there — the terminal equivalent of right-click → New Folder, or Delete.

Deleting from a terminal is permanent — there's no Recycle Bin or Trash to rescue you afterward. Double-check the file or folder name before pressing enter, especially with anything that deletes a whole folder's contents at once.
blocks.title: No undo here

blocks.text: Reading a Command: Command, Flags, Arguments

blocks.html: Most commands follow the same shape: the command itself, optional flags that change how it behaves (usually starting with - or /), and an argument — what to actually act on.

blocks.code:
ls -la my-site
│   │   └─ argument: which folder to list
│   └─ flags: -l (long format) and -a (show hidden files too)
└─ command: list files

blocks.html: Once this shape clicks, an unfamiliar command stops looking like a magic word to memorize and starts looking like something you can actually read — a command, adjusted by flags, aimed at an argument.

blocks.text: Running a Program from the Terminal

blocks.html: Instead of double-clicking a file, you can tell the terminal to run it directly by naming the program that understands it, followed by the file: python app.py runs a Python file, node app.js runs a JavaScript file. This is how nearly every real project actually gets started, once you're past the code editor.

blocks.alt: Isometric diagram of a terminal window with an arrow pointing to a gear and play button icon, representing a program being launched from a typed command
blocks.caption: Typing python app.py or node app.js hands the file to that program and runs it — the same idea as double-clicking, just typed instead of clicked.

blocks.html: Two errors show up constantly for beginners, and neither means anything is broken:

rows: That program isn't installed yet, or the terminal doesn't know where to find it
You're trying to change something the current user account isn't allowed to touch

blocks.text: Why Every Developer Ends Up Here

blocks.html: A GUI can only offer the buttons someone thought to build. The terminal can do anything the computer is capable of, which is why tools like Git, Python, and Node.js are all typed, not clicked. The next two lessons — Git and GitHub — are typed entirely from here.

blocks.alt: An infographic covering command line and terminal basics — GUI vs CLI, opening a terminal on Windows and macOS, navigation commands, creating and deleting files, and reading a command's structure
blocks.caption: The same commands, side by side for Windows and macOS/Linux — the exact reference used throughout the Cybersecurity course's CLI lessons too.
